title: Can You Get Out Of My Rope?
description: In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky share a tension-filled rope game called ‘Can You Get Out of My Rope?’.
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky share a tension-filled rope game called ‘Can You Get Out of My Rope?’.

Tension is one of the most important elements of rope bondage but what exactly does this mean and what does good tension in ropes look (and feel) like? As Lief explains, one of the most common mistakes many riggers make early on in their rope journeys is tying too loosely. In this fun and beginner-friendly rope game, you can start developing a hands-on feeling for tying with proper tension with no knots, no frictions, only one rope, and the challenge: can you get out of my rope?

This exercise is both suitable and recommended for beginners. With both a ‘simple’ and a ‘harder’ version demonstrated, try the variation that best suits your practice until, well, tension comes easy.

title: Coconut Rope
description: In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky offer a deep dive into the risks and rewards of playing with coconut rope, as well as techniques.
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky offer a deep dive into the risks and rewards of playing with coconut rope, as well as techniques for utilizing it on the floor or in suspensions.

Mean, scratchy, messy, difficult to handle and impossible to break in, coconut rope will shred your fingers, shed all over your floor and insult your mother. Of course, what makes coconut rope so challenging to tie with is also a large part of what makes it such a fun tool for sensation play in shibari – if you know how. In this series, Lief and Icky detail what to expect from this rough and unwieldy fiber, including the very real safety considerations for both bottoms and riggers, and how these should influence how you use and apply it.

In the first video, they offer advice for the basic handling of coconut rope, using a futomomo tie as an example for how to place it on the body, as well as sharing their tips for the kinds of applications coconut rope is and isn’t suitable for.

In the second video, they demonstrate how even just one hank of coconut rope can be used to create a compression chest harness, exploring both breath play and sensation play in one mean-but-minimalist tie.

In the third video, you’ll see how coconut rope can be used to create a tengu tie for more sadistic floor play.

In the final video, Lief and Icky offer insights for how coconut rope can be used in suspensions – not for load-bearing structures or uplines, but to add sensation and intensity under your other suspension-suited fibers.

This course offers guidance for how coconut rope can be used at every level of your rope practice. However, due to the risks involved, it’s important to be absolutely certain that playing with it falls within your risk profile as well as that of your tying partner/s. Start slow and always keep your skill set in mind.

title: General Rope Safety (Free)
description: A free course that helps evaluate and navigate potential risks associated with Shibari.
about:
In this free shibari safety course, Lecia gives you a general overview of the most relevant aspects you should understand before starting your bondage practice. This includes information about different types of rope, cutting tools, anatomical knowledge – especially about nerves and nerve damage symptoms – but also consent and communication, self-reflection, psychological aspects and pain processing strategies.

Although this course aims to be as exact as possible, you might find varying viewpoints and information when doing your own research. This course does not aim to provide definitive answers or absolute truths about the topics covered, but rather to guide you and encourage you to consider and investigate further on all of these important safety topics.

With this course, we wish to help you better understand, evaluate and navigate the potential risks associated with shibari in order for you to enjoy safer and more satisfying experiences in or with ropes.

title: Positioning Between Partners
description: In this shibari course, hua hua teaches a series of classes exploring how positioning between partners can influence your ties and sessions.
about:
In this shibari course, hua hua teaches a series of classes exploring how positioning between partners can influence your ties and sessions, with input from her model Olivia.

Think ‘position’ in shibari and you’re likely to imagine it’s all about the model and the shapes achieved in the course of the tie. As hua hua explains, though, while we might think less often of how the rigger is positioned in response to the bottom, it can still greatly affect the mood and experience of your rope sessions. Before you even lay the first rope, your starting positions can begin to communicate intent, create a sense of vulnerability or dominance, and allow you to introduce more or less challenge early on.

In the first class, hua hua explains the benefits and drawbacks of beginning your sessions seated or starting them standing. As she says, starting seated can help establish a greater sense of ease and intimacy; standing offers more space and options to play with proximity.

In the second class, hua hua explores how the rigger’s positioning behind, beside or in front of the bottom can be used to enhance engagement, amplify power exchange, or simply be more or less practical for different types of play.

In the final class, two seated starting options for bottoms are compared: kneeling (or seiza position) and cross-legged (or agura).

This course is suitable – and enocouraged – for all levels, and will help you approach your tying sessions with greater awareness and intention.

title: Tempo and Tension
description: In this shibari tutorial, Tifereth and her model Irkalla delve into how to use tempo and tension to weave intention into your scenes.
about:
Drama! Intrigue! Suspense! In this shibari tutorial, Tifereth and her model Irkalla delve into how to use tempo and tension to weave greater intention and emotional impact into your rope scenes.

Conveying your intention as a rigger is about more than just the active parts of the tying process. As queen of dramatic rope performances Tifereth explains, so much of the story lives in the pauses, in the shifts of rhythm, breath and eye contact, in the use of space and control of the flow of time. In the classes that follow, she explains how to begin working these concepts into your own rope practice.

In the first class, Tifereth and Irkalla demonstrate a rope-free drill focused on helping you develop a sense of intimacy, connection and shared purpose with your tying partner. Tifereth’s advice? Start slowly, gradually add movement and try to match each other’s intention. And while you’re at it, don’t default to the tying partner always being the leading partner – there’s a lot to be learned from following too.

In the second class, Tifereth demonstrates the evocative power of timing, tempo and how and when you play with pauses – both for communication intention to the person in your ropes as well as, in the case of performance rope, to an audience.

In the final class, the speed and pressure of your rope application join this heady mix, with practical advice for how to create high intensity on an emotional level without creating unsafe physical tension in your ties.

This class is appropriate for all levels, and is ideal for performance rope or anyone wanting to level up connection, intention and “interesting emotional consequences” in their rope scenes.

title: Motion & Intention
description: In this class, Gorgone discusses the importance of posture, movement, body language and spatiality in a rope session.
about:
In this class, Gorgone discusses the importance of posture, movement, body language and spatiality in a rope session with their model Alma.

How you choose to place yourself around your partner, finding your points of balance and imbalance, exploring each other's centre of gravity and being intentional about how you move your own and your partner's body will greatly affect the mood of your rope scenes.

Everyone's body and mobility is different, so it is important to explore and develop your own language. This class doesn't aim to tell you what to do or not to do, but rather to invite you to explore this communication tool and find what works for you and your partners.

Shibari is not about "rope - on the body" but about "the body - in rope".

Much as you don’t need a suspension point or advanced skills to start exploring fun and rewarding rope play, you don’t need a huge rope kit either. As Lief explains in this class, there are many ways to play with a single rope and to effectively use one rope to manipulate the whole body. One Rope Rodeo is a game that challenges you to make smarter and more efficient choices as a rope top and to think about placement, position and even out-of-the-box adaptations to make a single hank of rope go a long way...

This floor-based tying exercise is suitable for all levels, as long as you allow your own skill set to guide you. There are lots of follow-along patterns out there but it’s games like this that create a foundation for creative, flexible and engaging tying.

about:
In this course, Gorgone teaches three separate “capture ties” with their model Lexi.

Unlike many more structured ties, these fun, quick and infinitely adaptable ties focus on using the body to lock itself instead of using a lot of rope to lock the body. Each tie starts with a lark’s head instead of a single-column tie meaning there’s very little technique involved, so they’re very simple to achieve as well as being ultra-efficient.

These beginner-friendly capture ties are perfect for dynamic play with the concept lending itself to plenty of further experimentation and exploration.

title: Ichinawa | One Rope Play (Free)
description: Tying with one rope only is often called Ichinawa, from the Japanese "ichi" (one) and "nawa" (rope).
about:
Tying with one rope only is often called Ichinawa, from the Japanese "ichi" (one) and "nawa" (rope). In this video, Gorgone demonstrates in a short session with her model Jewerlyandfire what can be done with a single rope by using and combining the concepts and techniques that she teaches in the Shibari Beginner Course.

Shibari can be highly technical and intricate but before loosing ourselves in the fancy techniques, we should remember that bondage can also be a sensual, playful and emotional practice. The rope is an extension of our body. We can use it to restrain, move, pull, push, squeeze... It can be soft and gentle like a caress or rough and assertive. The panel of sensations and emotions available is infinite!

Rope is only a tool to communicate; it’s the language, not the subject. The key elements of a rope dialogue are rhythm (fast/slow), space (close/far) and tightness (strong/soft). Pauses and variations of those elements are important to keep the dialogue dynamic and interesting.

In this impactful discussion, Reemah, Anansi, and Lavender discuss being BIPOC in rope, rope spaces, and kink communities. They deep dive into the important nuances that exist at the intersectionalities of race and kink.

As Reemah, Anansi, and Lavender explain, for people of color, (particularly Black people) the experience of navigating kinky communities and playing with rope asks for greater awareness, intentionality, and inclusion as an active process. Topics covered range from understanding the importance of trauma-informed kink for BIPOC practitioners, and how to begin meaningful conversations about developing accessibility in rope, to how engaging in kink can be a type of reclamation. This insightful conversation explores how each facet of rope bondage and kink can be approached more mindfully to ensure that rope is truly inclusive of all people.

title: Safety 101 (Free)
description: A foundational introduction to safety essentials for your rope bondage practice.
about:
In this shibari course, fuoco, Kinknamepending and Shakti Bliss present Safety 101, a foundational introduction to safety essentials for your rope bondage practice.

As you start your rope journey, even your earliest ties will require you to make choices about risk, safety, and consent. This series is all about taking the guesswork out of those decisions and laying the groundwork for an informed, risk-aware practice. From choosing your materials to physical safety to consent and negotiation, a safer rope experience starts here.

First up, let’s talk equipment as fuoco presents three classes all about ropes. Here, you’ll learn the pros and cons of different types of rope, how to treat jute rope (the type of rope you see in every Shibari Study tutorial), and how to bundle and store your ropes to better ensure their longevity.

In the next two videos, Pen and fuoco share an introduction to rope injuries that could show up in the early part of your rope journey. From rope marks and rope burn to injuries due nerve compression, falling, and sustained stressful positions, they offer advice on what to expect as well as how to mitigate risk as you tie. Central to safer shibari for beginners? Careful rope placement that avoids more vulnerable areas of the body.

Finally, Shakti and Pen introduce you to consent, first as a somatic journey that starts with you – identifying what you want and whether you’re comfortable asking for it – and then as a practice of ongoing negotiation and communication between tying partners.

This shibari safety series is aimed specifically at beginners who are just starting out, though you’re welcome to come back any time to brush up on the basics.

This series is suitable and recommended for all levels. Building a framework for effective communication in ropes and learning how to refine it will always benefit your shibari, no matter where you are in your journey.

title: Nerve Safety For Rope Bondage
description: In this rope bondage tutorial series, Cait teaches a six-part course on nerve safety in ropes with their model Gigi.
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Cait teaches a six-part course on nerve injury and nerve safety in ropes with their model Gigi.

Nerve injuries are one of the most common injuries we see in rope bondage. As the connections between body and brain, damage to nerves can be debilitating, which is why risk-aware rope play is so essential. This multi-class series is focused not only on raising awareness about where the most common injuries occur but also on providing insights into how to lower the risk of nerve injuries and how to handle them when they do occur.

The first class offers an overview of the anatomy of a nerve and how to tell the difference between nerve damage and circulation loss.

In the second and third videos, Cait discusses the nerves of the upper and lower body respectively, with a special focus on those most commonly affected in rope bondage.

The fourth part of the course focuses on the mechanisms of nerve injuries, particularly with regard to compression and shearing injuries, which are most commonly seen in shibari.

The fifth class examines some of the known risk factors that might may increase your likelihood of nerve injury in ropes as well as how you can begin to mitigate some of those risks.

Finally, the last video offers invaluable advice on how to handle a nerve injury if it occurs.

This course is suitable for all levels with indispensable information for both riggers and rope bottoms alike. Whether you’re just starting out or looking to refresh your nerve knowledge, we advise you to keep coming back to this information throughout your practice.

Cait has prepared an amazing and highly comprehensive hand-out to supplement the content taught in their class. This is a complementary tool with the class. Click here to download and familiarize yourself extensively with its contents about nerves.

Please be aware that this is not professional medical advice. We encourage everyone to research this topic further and to always consult your primary care physician when in doubt.

about:
In this casual shibari-inspired discussion session, Ms. Reemah, Anansi and Lavender explore the ins, outs and absolute essentials of consent and negotiation.

Consent is the power of your ‘yes’ or your ‘no’, explains Ms. Reemah. Negotiation in ropes, on the other hand, goes into the nuances of ‘what’, ‘how’ and ‘when’. Both consent and negotiation are essential elements of every rope scene – whether you’re tying with someone new, learning at a shibari workshop or playing with a long-established tying partner.

In the course of this conversation, three experienced rope practitioners and occasional tying partners share an engaging discussion filled with both funny anecdotes and profound insights into what consent and negotiation may look and sound like in a real-life rope practice. From the early stages of vetting potential new rope partners to the concept of ‘continuous negotiation’ during tying to how we wrap up our play with aftercare, this deep dive into consent and negotiation is all about fostering safer, more responsible and more rewarding play in ropes.

This discussion is suitable – and encouraged – for all levels.

title: The Ice Game: Tools For Pain Processing
description: In this shibari skills class, Margherita and Shakti Bliss expand your toolbox for processing pain and navigating intense sensations.
about:
In this shibari skills class, Margherita and Shakti Bliss expand your toolbox for processing pain and mindfully navigating intense sensations with a chilly hands-on exercise: the Ice Game.

Ever noticed how you hold your breath when anticipating something difficult? Or sigh in relief at a good outcome? What about the deep-in-your-belly moans you let out in a hard tie or the way you find yourself unconsciously gripping onto something as you try to manage discomfort? As Margherita and Shakti explain, our bodies tend to know how to process intense sensations without instruction. This class is all about identifying and honing these tools for self-regulation for better use when we need them, in or out of ropes. And because your body needs time to absorb and digest these skills, don’t wait until your next rope session to practice: the Ice Game is the perfect low-stakes way to get started and a safe way to play with challenging sensations.

This class is suitable for all levels and roles. Whether you’re a rope bottom looking to exercise somatic skills or a top looking for insights into emotional processing, this is your chance to have some fun and take away essential tools in the process.

title: Kinoko's Performance Theory
description: In this insightful discussion, Kinoko expands on how he approaches shibari performances.
about:
In this insightful discussion, Kinoko expands on how he approaches shibari performances, where he finds his inspiration and how he views his role within the shibari community.

Rope bondage fans across the globe are familiar with Kinoko as an icon of the shibari world. Perhaps less familiar though are the thought processes and traditional art forms that, these days, play an influential role in Kinoko’s performances. From ikebana (the Japanese art of flower arranging) to Japanese calligraphy, Kinoko reveals how his appreciation for these art forms has informed his rope practice and performance philosophy.

In the second part, Kinoko shares his view on the intricate nature of connection within shibari and explores the complexities of maintaining respect for personal relationships.

If you loved this deep dive into Kinoko’s inspiration, conceptualization and creative process around his performances, make sure you don’t miss his captivating Traditional Performance with model hua hua.

title: Context & Characteristics
description: In this rope bondage class, Anna Bones delves deeper into the context and characteristics that inform what we call ‘shibari’.
about:
In this rope bondage class, Anna Bones delves deeper into the context and characteristics that inform what we call ‘shibari’.

What do we mean when we speak about ‘shibari’ and how does this differ from other types of bondage? And beyond the words we use, how can rope itself be used as a tool to communicate our intent? This theoretical class is the perfect starting point to understand why we tie the way we tie, why we use the tools we use, and how these – and not the ‘end result’ of a specific harness or pattern – are some of the most rewarding aspects of the practice.

This class is aimed at beginners and those with an interesting in bondage looking to start expanding their understanding of the whys and the hows of shibari.

title: Rope as a Language
description: This rope bondage series By Anna Bones provides the foundations for your bondage practice.
about:
In this rope bondage series, Anna Bones explores some of the fundamentals for bringing nuance and awareness to your tying practice with her model Nuur.

In the first class, ‘Rope as a Language’, Anna teaches how to simple rope and body handling techniques can make a serious difference in your tying sessions. After all, when it comes to rope bondage, knowing how to tie various knots and frictions is just one part of the practice. Arguably as important is knowing how to handle your rope and understanding how different ways of using speed, tension and tempo can create different sensations and even emotions for your partner, so setting the tone for various types of play. During the course of the class, Anna shares her insights into how rope can be a form of communication.

In the second class, ‘Form and Ropes’, Anna teaches the fundamentals of tying with the contours of your partner’s body. Learning good tying habits early on will put you on an advantageous footing as your bondage practice advances. One such habit is understanding that the idea is not to place your rope in straight lines across the body and starting to observe the shape of the body to guide your rope placement instead.

This class is dedicated helping beginners not only master this important skill but also understand why and how to apply it as they progress, with emphasis on tying the torso and hips. As Anna explains, this is an explorative exercise, akin to drawing on the body with the rope.

While this series is aimed at beginners, we encourage everyone to take some time to brush up on the basics. The foundations of your bondage practice are laid here.

title: Tying Different Bodies
description: In this shibari and anatomy tutorial series, Reemah discusses how the same types of ties can be adapted for different bodies.
about:
In this insightful shibari and anatomy tutorial series, Reemah discusses how the same types of ties can be adapted for different bodies with her models Anansi and Lavender.

Rope is not a one-size-fits-all practice. What works for one person’s body may be totally unsustainable or incorrectly placed on the next. In this essential course, Reemah offers useful guidelines for how to use the anatomy of the person being tied to determine your rope placement for various parts of the body, so making for more sturdy, sustainable and safer ties.

In the first video, Reemah advises on how to approach arms-front harnesses and how different chest sizes require adaptations in your placement.

In the second video, she discusses the rope placement of harness that bring the arms behind the back, such as the TK.

In the third video, Reemah demonstrates the same technique to find the waist for a waist rope on her two different models – resulting in two seemingly vastly different placements. As she emphasizes throughout the series, this is a function of adjusting your rope for the person being tied.

Finally, in the fourth video, Reemah explores thigh cuffs and the various anatomical factors that can help you tie better cuffs on any body you encounter.

This shibari tutorial series is appropriate and recommended for all levels. Better bondage begins with understanding that rope is a tool that can be adapted to any body, not the other way around.

In this series, you'll find a variety of common stretch positions. Each video is designed to help you understand what muscles are actually intended to stretch in various positions, and the ways in which flexibility limitations might show up in your rope practice. Use this as a starting point to develop greater body awareness in and out of rope, and as a tool to help you understand how to customize stretches to your own body in ways that still target the correct muscles.

In addition, you'll find the All About Shoulders videos. While these are not necessarily stretching videos, they are intended to expand your understanding of how shoulders work and draw your awareness to this joint, especially as it relates to determining what sort of harnesses work for you body.

title: Playing In The Dark
description: Bondagious and Thumper explore a nuanced approach to consent in shibari.
about:
In this discussion and demo, Bondagious and Thumper explore a nuanced approach to consent in shibari, designed to address the many complex sides of play that don’t fit into more binary models.

Our experiences in rope bondage are rarely as neatly categorized as “good” or “bad”. Some are unexpected but enjoyable, others challenging but welcome, and others still asked for and then entirely overwhelming. As Bondagious and Thumper explain, the “enthusiastic informed consent” model may be Kink 101, but it assumes our desires will always be transparent and easy to articulate. Their question: What lies in the shadows, and how can we expand our approach to consent to move beyond the moralistic and into more ambiguous spaces? Enter <slowly, and with caution> “playing in the dark”.

In the introductory discussion, Bondagious and Thumper offer a four-quadrant consent model designed to avoid categorizations of “positive” or “negative”, and instead based on whether elements of a scene are “invited/uninvited” and “welcome/unwelcome”.

In the delightfully titled ‘How to be gross without being gross’ class, the pair delve deeper into the limitations of conventional consent models. Additionally, they discuss how we can think about and mindfully begin to “fuck around and find out” when it comes to those elements that are unknown, unnameable, or unconscious.

In the rope session, playing in the dark takes a turn for the literal with a tying exercise focused on trusting without seeing, without knowing and without a clear idea of the outcome.

Finally, they offer a debrief on their blindfolded tying session, circling back to the themes of “invited/uninvited” and “welcome/unwelcome” and how they showed up in the tie.

This course is suitable for all levels. Keep in mind that exploring consent in this way may only come into play as your shibari practice progresses or as your rope partnerships deepen. There’s nothing wrong with sticking to enthusiastic informed consent if that’s best for your dynamic.

title: Being with Pain in Rope
description: Learn to explore pain in rope with confidence, using adaptable tools for regulation, intensity, connection, and body awareness.
about:
In this shibari skills class, Shakti Bliss and her tying partner Margherita share Being With Pain In Rope, an insightful exploration of sensation not as a problem to be solved, but as an invitation to listen.

If Shakti and Margherita’s chilly pain-processing Ice Game was all about recognizing the little ways in which your body inherently knows how to self-regulate and deal with discomfort, this exercise is about putting them into practice in ropes. The goal? Neither to avoid pain entirely nor to charge into challenging sensations carelessly. Somewhere in the middle is pain as a journey, and it’s this journey that you get to create or receive every time you play with ropes.

In the first video, Shakti shares two core perspectives that shed light on how we manage intense sensations: pain gate theory and turning inward. As she explains, the first is useful for “overwhelming” the brain with things that feel good – comfort, gentle touch, physical closeness. Alternatively, the second is all about surrendering to difficult sensations and finding the “little seed of ecstasy” at the nucleus of that suffering.

In the second video, Shakti and Margherita demonstrate how your shibari sessions are an opportunity to use both sets of tools – closeness and distance, relief and intensity – with advice on how to build up the intensity in increments. At the same time, Shakti details the subtle reactions she observes in Margherita, the little clues – sounds, breath, tension – of the work she’s doing as she processes the sensations of the tie.

This class is suitable for all levels. While they use a suspension for this example, Shakti emphasizes that this is not a copy-paste exercise, but rather a blueprint that can be adapted for experience, flexibility, body awareness and skill set, to meet your practice where it’s at.

This course utilizes suspension lines to create the final form. Before attempting, you’ll need to first familiarize yourself with safe suspension line technique and with the harnesses being used.

In this shibari tutorial, Fuoco explains the concept of ‘making rainbows’ in rope, with tips and pointers for how to avoid making rainbows but fold your rope instead for more efficient tying.

‌Oftentimes, better rope handling comes down to our most basic techniques and the good habits we’ve picked up along the way – or the bad ones we might not even realize are impacting our ties. In this beginner-friendly drills class, Fuoco focuses on ‘making rainbows’, a rope handling habit that can lead to uneven rope ends and less effective frictions. Then, using Munter hitches to demonstrate, she offers an alternative approach, folding the rope where it needs to turn, for better tie building.

This rope bondage course is suitable for beginner levels up and does not require a tying partner. We recommend that everyone spend some time drilling shibari fundamentals, no matter how advanced your practice.

title: Rolling The Dice
description: In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky share Rolling the Dice, a fun rope game to boost creativity and body manipulation skills.
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky share Rolling the Dice, another fun labbing-for-better-rope game, this time using dice to help you practice better body manipulation and get more creative in rope.

It’s time to take overthinking out of your rope and leave it to a roll of the dice. While memorizing various patterns and harnesses has its place in shibari, this playful game challenges riggers and bottoms to be creative, reimagine how various parts of the body can be connected, and get flexible (sometimes even literally). As Lief and Icky explain, each side of the dice correlates with a different body part – which parts is up to you and how you tie them together after rolling your dice is definitely up to you. Remember that you’re allowed to veto the dice too: if something doesn’t feel doable for whatever reason, you can always roll again.

This exercise is suitable for all levels, as long as you allow your own skill set to guide you. Thinking outside the box in your rope practice is a valuable skill at every level.

title: Speed Tying Drills
description: In this shibari course, Tifereth teaches a series of speed tying drills to help you tie more smoothly, fluidly, and quickly.
about:
In this shibari course, Tifereth teaches a series of speed tying drills with her model Irkalla. These exercises are designed to help you tie more fluidly, smoothly and – of course – quickly.

Smooth, fast and fluid tying can bring more energy and playfulness into your rope scenes and, as Tifereth explains, is an essential skill for rope performances. Test your coordination and concentration – and you’ll come out a better rigger for it.

This course is divided into three classes – watch and drill each, pausing in between to take as much time as you need to practice each exercise until you’re able to repeat it consistently, smoothly and confidently:

1 On the Move – One of the most important elements of smoother, faster tying is learning to move both the rope and yourself. This standing drill will get you in the habit of moving your feet and your lines simultaneously, while maintaining tension in your rope.

2 Magnet Hands – Imagine your hands are two magnets repelling each other, keeping your hands as far apart from each other as possible as you move and tie, and you’ll have a good basis for smooth and speedy rope handling. The challenging part of this drill? Once you’ve figured out keeping your hands apart, it’s time to learn to move your body in opposite direction to your rope.

3 Bundling – Once you’ve got the hang of the first two techniques, move onto the final drill where Tifereth demonstrates a technique to bundle as you move that allows for better control of your rope ends. This drill is the most challenging but stick with it, and when you’re ready to level up, try changing directions.

These rope bondage drills are suitable for anyone wanting to improve and speed up their rope handling and flow. You don’t even need a partner – these can be practiced around a pole or pillar too. We recommend that everyone spend some time drilling these skills, no matter how advanced your practice.

title: Geeking About The Single-Column Tie
description: In this shibari course, Fuoco teaches one of the most widely used and important fundamental ties in shibari with her model Cat: the SCT.
about:
In this shibari course, Fuoco takes a deep dive into one of the most widely used and important fundamental ties in shibari with her model Cat: the single-column tie (SCT).

Whether you’re still fairly new to shibari or you’ve been tying for a while, the single-column tie is likely one of the first ties you learnt and an invaluable building block in your rope practice. This four-part course is all about understanding how that building block works in order to use it as effectively as possible and ultimately make your single-column ties more robust and reinforced. With an in-depth exploration of various types of single-column tie, considerations for smarter tying with each, plus a game to test all your new single-column tie know-how, it’s time to get geeking…

The first class explores collapsible ties and parallel directionality. Square knot, granny knot, reef knot… Whatever you call them, this one is all about collapsible single-column ties and how your running line moves out of your cuff at a parallel.

Now that you’ve got the hang of parallel directionality, let’s add a twist. The second class is all about collapsible ties and perpendicular directionality and how to build sturdier ties when your running line takes a turn out of your cuff.

In the third class, Fuoco explores non-collapsible ties and perpendicular directionality, explaining why tying with directionality in mind still matters when you’re using Somerville bowlines or other forms of non-collapsible single-column tie.

Finally, in the last part of the course, it’s time for a game of Single-Column Tie Twister to test your skills.

This course is suitable for all levels, though some confidence with rope handling and experience tying single-column ties is beneficial.

title: Handling Drills For Flow
description: In this shibari course, Fuoco teaches a series of drills together with her model Cat.
about:
In this shibari course, Fuoco teaches a series of drills together with her model Cat. These tie-along videos are designed for you to return to time and again, any time your rope handling needs to be dusted off.

Learning patterns may be integral to your shibari journey but so is connecting with your partner. If exploring intent and connection tends to take a backseat to perfecting patterns, developing your rope handling skills is an easy way to level up without the need for a lot of new knots and frictions. Getting comfortable with these drills will help you to tie more smoothly, quickly and confidently, so you can give more of your attention to the person in your rope as you wrap them up.

Finger Hooking: In the first drill video, Fuoco discusses finger hooking technique and offers three variations of the same exercise, utilizing finger hooking skills and three different frictions to create a simple mermaid tie. You’re encouraged to follow along however works best for you. Tie along on a chair or table. Adapt the drill to tie your partner’s upper body once you feel comfortable with tying on the legs. Keep it interesting for yourself but just keep coming back!

Make a Stick: This drill video is all about how to pass rope between the body and other ropes with smoothness and ease. Follow along with Fuoco as she does the drill herself in real time. Notice if, with practice, you’re able to keep pace with her and see your rope handling skills improving! If you don’t have a model to practice with, this drill can absolutely be adapted to work on a piece of furniture or your own legs!

Control Your Rope Ends: As we begin to tie faster and with more confidence, rope ends tend to go flying, and these wild rope ends can be a hazard to both you and your bottom. No one likes being popped in the face with a rogue rope end, so learning to control all of your rope – down to your little stopper knots – is important. Join Fuoco as she guides you through a drill designed to help you gain better control of the whole length of your rope.

Laying Your Rope: A drill that can be practiced with a partner or on your own body, this exercise is designed to help you confidently lay rope on a body with even tension, and without twists or gaps. Follow along with Fuoco and Cat and practice laying your rope down well without needing to look at your every move, so that you can give more of your attention to your partner!

This class is suitable for all levels. Even very experienced riggers know the benefit of returning to basic handling drills from time to time. If you’re a total newbie, you might want to familiarize yourself with single column ties and basic frictions first. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own rope practice.

title: Feelings Game
description: In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky share their Feelings Game to help you and your tying partners build better communication when tying.
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky share one of their labbing-for-better-rope games to help you and your tying partners build better communication when tying: the Feelings Game.

The Feelings Game is an adaption of an exercise developed by the Devil Mask Society as part of their tying Cell curriculum. That curriculum is open source and can be found on their website: devilmasksociety.com

In shibari, we often speak of rope as a ‘language’ for communicating intent, so how do you make sure nothing gets lost in translation? As Lief and Icky explain, conveying and receiving feeling are the two halves of intent-driven, rewarding rope scenes, and building an effective communication practice and style will better help you feel, well, the things you want to feel. The Feelings Game is a fun and exploratory exercise in building a rope language together with your partner, combining pre-scene negotiation, non-verbal communication skills during tying and, of course, working to convey the desired emotion as clearly as possible.

This class is divided into three parts: a pre-scene negotiation where Icky expresses three feelings they would be open to feeling in ropes during the scene, the non-verbal tying session in which Lief picks one of the negotiated emotions to try to convey, and a debrief interview where we find out of Icky can guess which emotion Lief chose based on their tying alone.

This exercise is suitable for all levels, as long as you allow your own skill set to guide you. Effective communication in ropes doesn’t require complicated techniques or advanced skills – the more you play this game, the more you will come to learn just that!

Not sure what you want to feel in ropes today? Check out this list for some emotional inspiration.

title: Drills For Single-Column Ties
description: In this shibari tutorial series, Fuoco teaches a series of drill exercises to help you practice and perfect single-column ties.
about:
In this shibari tutorial series, Fuoco teaches a series of drill exercises to help you practice and perfect single-column ties.

The single-column tie (SCT) is one of the first ties anyone learning shibari will encounter. As one of the fundamental building blocks of your rope practice right from the get-go, it’s essential not to dismiss the humble SCT as basic or unimportant. As Fuoco explains in this course, even the best and most advanced riggers dedicate themselves to making their single-column ties smoother, faster and cleaner. These exercises are designed to help you do the same, by focusing some time and energy into constructing better single-column ties.

This shibari course is divided into five videos – watch and drill each, pausing in between to take as much time as you need to practice each exercise until you’re able to repeat it consistently smoothly and confidently:

1 Building the Wrap ­– tips and tricks for more efficient cuff construction.

2 Constructing the Loop – paying attention to how you fold your rope.

3 Theory and Locking the Cuff – understanding how the Somerville bowline works.

4 Switching Hands – okay, now learn how to do it all with your non-dominant hand taking the lead…

5 Switching Directions – once you’ve mastered switching hands, further develop your handling by tying the cuff in the other direction.

This rope bondage course is suitable for beginner levels up. We recommend that everyone spend some time drilling shibari fundamentals, no matter how advanced your practice.

title: Moving The Body
description: In this shibari course, hua hua teaches Moving the Body – without rope, with rope and in suspension – with her model Dantianshi.
about:
In this shibari course, hua hua teaches Moving the Body – without rope, with rope and in suspension – with her model Dantianshi.

Rope skills without body manipulation are fine if you, you know, want to turn your partner into an elaborately tied paperweight. But for finding your flow in shibari and moving the body with ease, you’ll need to understand body mechanics first. In this three-part class, hua hua offers a grounding in the core principles for moving your rope bottom smoothly, efficiently and without force, before showing how those principles can be applied tying on the ground and in the air.

In the first video, hua hua demonstrates how to move the body without ropes, based on where you apply force, what type of movement you use, and how weight distribution can be used to your advantage. As she explains, if you can do this with just your hands first, applying the same with rope will come more easily.

In the second video, hua hua invites you to see the rope tail as an extension of your hand, applying the concepts from the first class with rope in hand. Additionally, she offers tips for how to use opposing forces to guide the body, incorporating a suspension point, and more.

In the final video, moving the body in space is levelled up, literally. As hua hua explains, suspending supports the weight of the body, meaning less energy and effort and more movement potential. This class builds on the skills explored in the first two classes, with tips and tricks for position, suspension line placement, and how to create space for movement.

This course is suitable for various steps along the way in your shibari journey. The first class is ideal for beginners, the second for those with a little more tying and rope handling experience, while the last class is aimed at those with plenty of floor play experience who are beginning to explore suspensions. Keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from this course and only take your body manipulation skills into the air if that is already a part of your rope practice.

title: Fitness For Hyper Mobility (Free)
description: This body care and movement class teaches how to train and strengthen for hypermobility.
about:
Designed with the needs of hyper-mobile students in mind, in this body care and movement class for bendy bottoms, Fuoco walks us through training and strengthening for hypermobility.

Hypermobility simply means that you have a greater range of motion in some or all of your joints than most people and you can extend them easily and painlessly beyond what most others can – it’s frequently referred to as being “double-jointed” (no double joints involved though).

But wait, that sounds perfect for Shibari? The reality is although you’ll often hear of bottoms thinking that they’re not flexible enough for ropes, the other side of the suppleness spectrum isn’t necessarily all neat party tricks and contortions either. Those models whose flexibility is beyond the normal range – who are hypermobile – can sometimes be more susceptible to injury and joint dislocation than their less bendy counterparts.

This class will help you develop joint stability to support your active bottoming skills and protect your body on the long run. If this style of work is new to you, expect it to be frustrating at first. For many people, this will be the first time that you've asked your body to work in this way, and it's likely that you'll spend several sessions feeling like you're not making any progress at all when, in fact, you're building the brain-body connection necessary to perform these exercises.

title: Solo And Partnered Stretching
description: In this body conditioning tutorial, Ms Reemah and her model Lavender demonstrate a series of solo and assisted stretching exercises.
about:
In this body conditioning for shibari tutorial, Ms Reemah and her model Lavender demonstrate a series of solo and assisted stretching exercises.

It’s time to set aside your ropes and explore an entirely different take on ‘working out the kinks’ with two stretching tutorials designed for before and after your rope sessions. As Ms Reemah explains, while there’s no such thing as risk-free shibari, proper stretching and body care can help mitigate some of the physical risks of the practice and even help you connect more deeply with your tying partner (or yourself). With one class focused on solo stretching for riggers and one on partnered stretching for bottoms, giving care and attention to the muscle groups most used in rope can become an integral part of your scenes.

In the first class, Ms Reemah discusses the often-overlooked topic of stretching and conditioning for riggers. Offering examples of stretches she likes to do before and after rope sessions, she focuses on the hands, fingers and wrists, and – for safer lifting – the hips, legs and thighs.

In the second class, Ms Reemah and Lavender demonstrate how stretching can be incorporated into aftercare after your rope sessions. As well as gently addressing any body strain or tension that may have arisen maintaining challenging positions, this is an opportunity for rope partners to reconnect and decompress together post-play.

This shibari tutorial course is appropriate for all levels. As Ms Reemah advises, do what your body can do – these exercises are not intended to be followed exactly but rather to give you an idea of how to target some areas frequently employed in rope. Each body is different, so meet yours where it’s at mindfully in order to avoid injury.

Sharing both their pre-scene discussion and their post-scene feedback as well as the session itself, this is the collaborative, connective, somewhat challenging and entirely wholesome ropey three-way dreams are made of…

When we think of shibari, we usually picture it as taking place between two partners or, perhaps, even as a solo practice. We rarely see it portrayed as a group activity or imagine that there might be space in a topping/bottoming dynamic for three, but TrueBlue, Shakti Bliss and Margherita are here to challenge every one of those ideas with their co-tying performance. From an insightful pre-performance discussion detailing how they planned and approached the session to their giddy post-performance check-in (with high-fives all round) – and, of course, the performance itself – witness the warm, tender and connective power of rope times three.

This performance is suitable for all to watch and enjoy. As always, remain mindful of your own skill set and allow this class to inspire you accordingly.

In this beautiful demo session, Gestalta and their model Aleks present "Mayfly" - a performance piece they usually perform on stage for a live audience. Unlike our previous demo sessions, this sequence is not an improvised play session but a choreographed sequence.

A lot of the rope sequences designed for live performances tend to be fast paced, emphasising technical complexity and showcasing a lot of transitions in the air for maximum "wow" effect. Gestalta presents here a more humble and minimalistic choreography allowing the performers and their audience to fully experience and appreciate every moment leading to the final full suspension. The face-up position they chose for the climax of this show displays the body caught in between falling and floating, a poetic tribute to the paradoxical experience of Shibari.

Aside from giving you up-close-and-personal insights as to how their exploding Mayfly TK and Mayfly Suspension taught on this website are woven into play, this inspiration session also reveals the connection and dynamic created between rigger and bottom as Gestalta and Aleks move together through this simple but very poetic sequence.

title: Predicament Session (Free)
description: In this session, Fred Hatt and his model Briki demonstrate a free-tying predicament and discuss their experience.
about:
In this intense session, Fred Hatt and his model Briki demonstrate a free-tying predicament and discuss their experience playing with this specific style of rope bondage.

Predicaments are Fred’s favorite form of rope play. Endurance, impossible choices, and playing with his bottom’s headspace are the key ingredients in the equation. In this form of play, the rigger and model are working ‘against’ each other rather than with each other. Predicament bondage is a form of bondage play in which a person is restrained with the option of placing themselves in two equally but differently stressful positions. Both are sufficiently uncomfortable that the model is forced to shift after a time from one to the other, so enjoying the best (or 'worst') of both.

This demo is not a tutorial and is simply meant to inspire viewers by showing how to incorporate technical knowledge into playful sessions. In this session, Fred uses a Tengu Harness, a thin bamboo tied to the ankles to force the legs open and a Hair Tie (which can be replaced with a Rope Gag).

We hope this session inspires you and triggers your curiosity about Advanced Predicament play.

about:
In this spellbinding shibari performance, hua hua and her rope partner Dantianshi demonstrate the connective power of one-rope play.

“‘Ipponnawa’ means ‘one rope’,” explains hua hua. “Beyond the literal meaning, ipponnawa is a concept in shibari that was developed by the late master Yukimura Haruki. With one rope, the primary focus of the play is in its attention to communication and the interaction between each other to guide the scene. With this minimalistic approach to tying, one must make the most of every inch of the rope, and be more mindful about where you place the ropes. Ipponnawa is a reminder that you do not need much to have a profound and powerful experience in ropes.”

Playing with sensation, pacing, and closeness and distance, the performance offers an intimate glimpse of how even just one rope can be used with intent and purpose for immersive rope scenes. The performance is followed by a feedback interview with hua hua and Dantianshi as they discuss their impressions of the session.

title: Basic Knots By Gorgone
description: In this section Gorgone teaches the basic knots as well as simple wrappings and closing options with the leftover rope.
about:
In this class, Gorgone teaches the Single Column Tie and Double Column Tie, explains their different functions and when to use one to the other.

The only time full knots are used in shibari is to start a tie and create an anchor point onto a limb or a body part, for this we use two basic ties called Single Column Tie (SCT) and Double Column Tie (DCT). These knots are the most basic but also most important ones, they should be practiced until your hands are faster than your brain.

One of the most important thing when tying someone else is to make them feel that you can tie those first knots quickly and confidently so they can let go and enjoy. Ideally you should be able to do these basic ties without looking at your hands, so you can rely on muscle memory and focus on your partner rather than your knots.

If applied creatively to the body, these two knots and a few simple rope wrappings and shibari frictions are enough to create beautiful and playful ties!

title: Exposure And Closure
description: In this shibari course, Lief and Icky explore vulnerability through both exposure and closure in rope.
about:
In this shibari course, Lief and Icky explore vulnerability through both exposure and closure in rope. They offer lectures, structured exercises, and demonstrations of these concepts to help you understand how to bring intensity and intimacy to your own rope scenes.

Playing with vulnerability is a powerful tool for heightening emotion in ropes. As Lief and Icky explain, this series of classes is all about exploring the ins and outs of physical and psychological exposure in rope. The course is designed to offer an intentional framework for navigating this exciting – and often challenging – type of play, beginning with a lecture focused on defining vulnerability and accessible ways to get there in ropes, incrementally building up to more demanding scenes.

Following the lecture, Lief and Icky demonstrate three exercises that use the principles of exposure and closure to start building up your vulnerability-centered scenes: a ‘Naughty, Nice & Needs’ exercise that offers a practical and fun way of discussing desires; an ‘Ugly Vs. Pretty Rope’ demo that expands on what both ‘naughty’ and ‘nice’ could look like; and a ‘Closure’ exercise focused on untying and ‘putting the person in ropes together after we’ve taken them apart’.

Finally, in the Floor Demo, Lief and Icky put all these elements together for a beautifully connective rope scene that balances demand and reward, surrender and trust, and plays with the full and potent spectrum between exposure and closure.

For some fun-but-effective ties to inspire you to start exploring exposure and closure in your own practice, check out Fred Hatt’s Mini Arm Ties.

title: Peel Them Like Fruit
description: A playful course exploring exposure and restraint by creatively combining rope and clothing.
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Thumper and Bondagious present the only slightly ominously titled Peel Them Like Fruit, a playful course focused on rope bondage and clothing play.

What are you wearing? No, really… it might just be a more pertinent question for your next shibari session than you thought. In this multipart class, exposure and restraint are explored through the lens of creatively combining rope and clothing to create different sensations, emotions and trajectories for your rope scenes.

In the first video, Bondagious and Thumper introduce the concept of clothing play, delving into the purpose and meaning of the things we wear, and how we can play with that when we tie. As they explain, each garment will present different possibilities for how it can be incorporated into your ties, and while playing with clothing can absolutely be used to make someone feel exposed or vulnerable, it can also be affirming, euphoric and embellishing.

The second video offers an exercise to begin exploring clothing play with a virtually no-skills-needed tie placed on top of a men’s button up shirt. The purpose of this exercise? Taking “the long way round the barn” – purposefully slowing down, seeing how rope and fabric interact, gradually beginning to play with exposure, and exploring position, layers, distance, breath, touch – all subtle but powerful elements for creating imbalance and tension.

In the third video, you get to ditch the ropes entirely as Bondagious and Thumper demonstrate how clothing alone can be an effective and intriguing tool for bondage – both partnered and even solo. Who knew you could hog-tie yourself with just a T-shirt?

In the fourth video, all the techniques and concepts from the first three classes are combined in a clothing-and-rope bondage sequence that gradually builds up in intensity, intentionally alternating between feelings of security and insecurity, before offering tips for how even “redressing” can become a core part of the scene.

Finally, the pair debrief after the tying session, reflecting on the various themes clothing play can amplify in rope, and offering guidance and important considerations for safer and more aware explorations.

This course is suitable for all levels, focusing less on technique and more on reimagining what we wear as another element that can be incorporated into our ropey play. Please keep your skill set in mind as you apply the concepts taught in this course to your own practice.

In this three-part shibari course, hua hua discusses the many benefits of tying slowly with her model Olivia.

Impactful rope bondage is about more than just technical skill. Rope handling, pacing, being able to read your rope partner’s reactions and being able to respond accordingly are important elements that can all affect the flow and feel of a scene. In this class, hua hua makes a case for slowing down when you tie – to make space for observing, for ongoing consent, for finding inspiration, for processing and for being able to identify when a tie may need to be modified or changed – and offers suggestions of when and where to pause. As hua hua explains, intentionally slowing your pace is not only a powerful tool for creating a more intense mood, it also helps to mitigate some of the communication and safety issues that may arise from tying in a rush.

This class is applicable to all levels, from beginner to expert. Every practice can benefit from a more intentional and nuanced approach to tying; how and where you apply it will depend on your own skill set, so remain mindful of where you are at and allow this class to inspire you accordingly.

Tying someone in a way that feels secure, connective and effective doesn’t have to mean complicated patterns or advanced rope skills. This series is all about taking the simplest route from zero to tied-up with no more than a single-column tie – the simplest way to start a tie – and the basic principles of tension (in other words, how tight you tie).

In the first class, you’ll be introduced to the concept of tension – a word that can carry many meanings in the context of a rope scene.

In the second class, you’ll meet the mighty single-column tie (SCT) – a fundamental tie that you’ll use throughout your shibari practice. While there are many ways to tie them, this class will introduce you to two of the easiest options, as well as offering practical safety advice for each.

In the final two classes, Margherita and Blue demonstrate how just a single-column tie + tension can be applied to both the upper and the lower body, highlighting different anatomical considerations as well as beginner rope handling techniques.

title: Understanding Rope For Bottoms Who Don’t Tie
description: In this shibari series, Fuoco discusses why it’s beneficial for bottoms to have a good grasp of how rope works and how being tied should.
about:
In this series of rope bondage classes, Fuoco, together with her model Enna, discusses why it’s highly beneficial for bottoms to have a good grasp of how rope works and how being tied should and shouldn’t feel.

Understanding how rope works is an incredibly useful bottoming skill that's rarely taught for the purpose of better bottoming. Understanding the basics of how rope works can help empower bottoms to independently assess the skill level of riggers they'd like to tie with and make collaborative decisions about what sort of rope to do together. Additionally, it can make for more constructive feedback and even collaborative problem-solving when things aren't working, allowing the person being tied to better understand where an issue may be arising rather than seeing themselves or their body as the problem.

In the first class in the course, Fuoco explores tension in ropes, demonstrating how a harness with good tension should look and feel versus one with poor tension.

The second class focuses on frictions with Fuoco providing important information about the specific purpose of frictions within a tie as well as demonstrating examples of how to visually assess whether or not a friction is doing its job.

The third video of this series looks at balance in terms of both symmetry and the ability of a tie to distribute load evenly. In this class, Fuoco offers valuable advice for both how to see and feel if a tie is imbalanced.

Finally, in the fourth class, Fuoco discusses how visually assessing up-lines can be an essential tool to help assess a potential rigger’s suspension readiness or their confidence in suspensions, with tips for easy-to-check features of suspension lines.

The goal of this series is to help bottoms, especially those who don't tie or are new to rope, determine what sort of rope they feel comfortable engaging in with a new-to-them partner. As such, this course is suitable for beginners and may also be helpful for riggers who are just starting out too. We encourage you to always keep your skillset in mind and always adopt a ‘low and slow’ approach if you are new to shibari.

title: Why Do Rope? (Free)
description: The purpose of this introductory rope class is to reflect on what brought you here.
about:
In this shibari class, Shakti Bliss, TrueBlue and Margherita dive into answering the all-important question for anyone just starting to learn shibari: why do rope?

Chances are, if you’ve landed here, that there’s something about rope bondage that intrigues you – maybe it’s something you’ve tried before, something you want to try or something you’ve always wondered about. The purpose of this introductory rope class is to reflect on what brought you here, and also to remind you that your ‘why’ in ropes may change with time. Just as there are many routes into rope bondage, so there are endless pathways to explore within it: your intention may change with experience, different partners, and even when tying yourself. As well as exploring the different roles in shibari based on whether you’re doing the tying or being tied, this discussion also encourages an expansive understanding of the motivations that bring people to rope – it’s a more versatile tool than you might think.

This discussion is suitable for all levels and encouraged for anyone just starting out. Write down or share your intentions with your rope partners and revisit them as your practice grows and progresses. This class forms part of our Getting Started curriculum.
safety: This class is suitable for all levels. It’s part of our Getting Started series, which we recommend you watch in order.

title: Wrapping the Body: Part 2 (Free)
description: Exploring how to add structure when wrapping the body and how to tie a more sustainable single-column tie.
about:
In this beginner shibari class, TrueBlue and her model Shakti Bliss build on foundational rope bondage skills, exploring how to add structure when wrapping the body and how to tie a more sustainable single-column tie.

A basic single-column tie and forward tension may be all you need to tie someone up; this class takes those bondage basics and levels them up to help you create more stable and structural ties. Additionally, as your rope skills grow, so do your options for interpersonal connection – as well as tie-along segments, Blue and Shakti share creative prompts for putting these techniques into practice and thinking about how you’re relating to each other in the process.

In the first class, Blue demonstrates how to tie a granny knot – a secure and compact way to finish your single-column ties.

In the second class, reverse-tension and friction join your growing tension toolbox to give your ties increased stability and staying power.

In the last two classes, Blue and Shakti demonstrate what using these techniques in a tie might look like with a focus on both rope handling and the interpersonal experience you can create.

This class is designed for shibari beginners and forms part of our Getting Started curriculum.
safety: This class is suitable for all levels. It’s part of our Getting Started series, which we recommend you watch in order.
equipment: At least one hank of rope

title: Hojo Cuffs
description: An introduction to the hojo cuff or inline column tie.
about:
In this beginner shibari class, TrueBlue and her model Shakti Bliss teach an introduction to the hojo cuff or inline column tie.

You’ve started a tie with a single-column tie… Now what? As Blue explains, this is where a hojo cuff might come in handy – a tie designed to use stable tension to capture and connect columns without the rope becoming too tight or unsustainable.

In the first part of the course, Blue demonstrates how to tie a hojo cuff.

In the videos that follow, Blue and Shakti demonstrate an agura (cross-legged) tie and an upper body box tie position utilizing a hojo cuff, exploring how just this simple technique can make seemingly complex-looking ties much more accessible.

Finally, they offer an inspirational demo, moving in and out of various shapes that can be achieved with hojo cuffs. As they explain, this is not for you to follow along, but rather to show the hojo cuff’s versatility in your earliest ties.

This class is intended for shibari beginners and forms part of our Getting Started curriculum.
safety: This class is suitable for all levels. It’s part of our Getting Started series, which we recommend you watch in order.

title: First Patterns (Free)
description: Step-by-step instructions for building your first patterns in rope.
about:
In this beginner shibari class, Shakti Bliss and her model TrueBlue share step-by-step instructions for building your first patterns in rope.

As you begin to bring intention, form and function to your first shibari ties, your fundamental knots and frictions become essential bondage building blocks. This class introduces learners to the double-column tie (DCT), detailing how just a DCT and half-hitches can already create structured and beautiful patterns.

In the first part of the class, you’ll learn how to tie a double column tie, as well as understanding the decision-making involved in how to start a tie.

The next two classes build upon that double-column tie, demonstrating how to tie a calf binder on the legs, or a forearm binder on the arms, as well as the different considerations to be kept in mind for different parts of the body. As the ties are built up, Shakti explains many of the useful rope handling techniques to be picked up along the way to maintain tension and create ease.

This class is intended for shibari beginners and forms part of our Getting Started curriculum.

title: Playtime: Maximalism
description: A maximalism-themed playtime session that asks: how many ropes can we put on?
about:
In this shibari demonstration and discussion, Margherita and her model TrueBlue share a maximalism-themed playtime session that asks: how many ropes can we put on?

One of the earliest lessons you’re likely to learn in your shibari journey is that it only takes a few fundamental skills and a single rope to effectively tie someone up… But why stop at just one rope? This inspirational tying session is all about exploring how, with even just beginner techniques, you can use plenty of rope to create ties that are all about constriction, sensation and connection.

In the first part of the class, Margherita demos how to join two ropes, an essential technique when you’re building ties that require multiple ropes.

In the second part of the class, Margherita and Blue discuss important considerations for this unstructured and “maximalist” approach to rope, particularly regarding safety and communication. As they say, the idea is not to tie along or recreate their tie, but to explore collaborative planning and creating your own with your rope partner.

In the third part of the class, Margherita and Blue share their maximalism session, talking through the process, decision-making and experience as they tie.

Finally, after the ropes have come off, the pair share their feedback and impressions of the session, a reminder that no matter how many ropes, good bondage is still – first and foremost – about remaining attentive to the person and not just the ropes.

This inspiration session is intended for shibari beginners and forms part of our Getting Started curriculum.
safety: This class is suitable for all levels. It’s part of our Getting Started series, which we recommend you watch in order.
equipment: At least two hanks of rope

title: Movement in Rope
description: How to move the body in ropes while keeping things as safe, efficient and collaborative as possible.
about:
In this beginner shibari tutorial, Margherita and her model Shakti Bliss explore how to move the body in ropes while keeping things as safe, efficient and collaborative as possible.

Moving another person’s body in space can be influenced by many different factors: body size, flexibility, position and more. Add ropes, and yet another variable is added to the equation, but there are ways to do it that reduce how much force you need to apply, how much weight either partner needs to support, and that will add fluidity to your rope scenes. The idea? Not just smoother movement and less risk of injury, but more connective and intentional play too.

In the first class, they offer a framework for understanding body mechanics and then using them to your advantage, demonstrating various techniques without ropes.

In the second class, the challenge is levelled up with the addition of ropes. The aim of this demo is to emphasize how restricting different body parts impacts mobility, and how to adjust for these new considerations.

This class is intended for shibari beginners and forms part of our Getting Started curriculum.
safety: This class is suitable for all levels. It’s part of our Getting Started series, which we recommend you watch in order.
equipment: At least one hank of rope

title: Playtime: Tension
description: A tension-themed playtime session designed to take fundamental technical skills and put them into practice.
about:
In this shibari demonstration and discussion, Margherita, Shakti Bliss and TrueBlue share a tension-themed playtime session designed to take fundamental technical skills and put them into practice in the most impactful way possible.

“Basic” or “easy to tie” don’t necessarily equate to basic or easy when you’re the person in ropes. This inspirational rope session is not a tie-along class but instead is intended to showcase some of the challenging experiences you can start to mindfully create with even just the tension of your ropes. Think breath play, sensory deprivation and more!

In the first part of the course, Margherita offers a bottom-centric perspective on the breath in ropes, and how you can adapt your breathing when restricted.

In the second part, Shakti and Margherita begin to explore wrapping for breath play, offering perspectives from each side of the dynamic on how to start playing with restriction through rope tension.

In the third part, Blue wraps Margherita’s head and face, explaining how the addition of ropes here can both affect breath and sensory input, as well as highlighting important safety considerations when tying this delicate area.

Finally, the trio debrief after the ropes have come off, offering feedback, insights into their decision-making while tying, and how mindfulness and intention showed up during the session.

This inspiration session is intended for shibari beginners and forms part of our Getting Started curriculum.
safety: This class is suitable for all levels. It’s part of our Getting Started series, which we recommend you watch in order.
equipment: At least two hanks of rope

title: First Flight Futomomo
description: In this shibari tutorial, Fuoco teaches the First Flight Futomomo with her model Enna.
about:
GO TO FIRST FLIGHT FUTOMOMO HARNESS GUIDE

In this shibari tutorial, Fuoco teaches the First Flight Futomomo with her model Enna.

“The perfect futomomo doesn’t exi—” Okay, okay, maybe the perfect futomomo doesn’t exist, but as you’ll see, the First Flight Futomomo checks plenty of boxes. As Fuoco explains, it’s an especially good option if you’re looking for a variation to begin trying to tie during suspensions. While more rope may make a futumomo more robust and comfortable, less makes it easier to tie in the air: this one happily meets somewhere in the middle, being built for both supportiveness and ease of getting on swiftly.

During the class, Fuoco offers options for how to start, based on your own preference, and step-by-step instructions for how to build the tie, as well as tensioning tips for maximum sustainability.

This course is great for anyone looking for a go-to futomomo for play in the air or on the ground. However, please keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from this class and only use this harness in suspension if that is already a part of your rope practice.

title: Kinoko's Bedroom Bondage
description: In this shibari tutorial series, Kinoko teaches two harnesses that can be used in the bedroom (and beyond), together with his model hua hua.
about:
In this shibari tutorial series, Kinoko teaches two harnesses that can be used in the bedroom (and beyond), together with his model hua hua.

Many beginner shibari learners first become interested in rope for its erotic applications, and while advanced suspensions and intense rope scenes may end up having their place in your practice, they’re not exactly bedroom-friendly. In this course, Kinoko teaches his take on shibari for sex with two ties that are straightforward, functional and fun. Importantly, Kinoko emphasizes that these harnesses are designed for comfort, sustainability and, well, the high likelihood of getting distracted during this type of play. As such, they’re easy to tie and untie and can be tied more loosely than some other shibari harnesses.

In the first video, Kinoko teaches an arms-front harness that plays with the feelings of being restrained while also being an easy position for the person being tied to maintain over a longer period.

In the second video, Kinoko offers a hip harness variation built for grabbing, tugging and pulling in all sorts of positions while still being simple to tie and comfortable to be in.

The third video offers pointers for how these harnesses can be used for play, making for bedroom bondage that mitigates the risks of more advanced ties while still being playful, intimate and spicy.

This class is suitable for beginner levels and beyond. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own rope practice. Remember, too, that consent and negotiation are integral to all types of rope play. Before beginning to experiment with these ties, decide in advance how you will use these harnesses, check in regularly during and remember that play can be stopped at any time if either partner feels uncomfortable.

title: Tengu Harness
description: In this class, Tamandua teaches his variation of the Tengu. This tie is a modern Shibari harness that is inspired by the wings of a demon.
about:
GO TO TAM’S TENGU HARNESS GUIDE

In this class, Tamandua teaches his variation of the Tengu with his model Mie Neko.

The Tengu (or “demon” tie) is a versatile modern Shibari harness, the position of which is inspired by the wings of the Tengu, mythological creatures featuring large wings.

Though the chest-opening position created by the Tengu accentuates vulnerability and exposure of the front body, it is, in fact, a very stable and sustainable tie that doesn’t require too much flexibility from the model and is suitable for all body types.

This harness is also perfectly suspendable, meaning that it can be utilized as an alternative to a TK, if they are not suited to your partner or if you'd like to try a different shape. This harness can be loaded from the front or back as demonstrated in the suspension video.

The harness alone is a suitable tie for intermediate level riggers, though using it for suspension is only advised for advanced practitioners. Tamandua also demonstrates another version of the Tengu for floor-play using bamboo in his series 'Semenawa Bamboo Ties'.

* Captions available for this series: English
safety: This is a harness course that requires the understanding of simple frictions and forms. It’s best practice to incorporate harnesses into your play only after you can tie them by memory. As rope crosses the arms in this course, we suggest the person being tied be familiar with how to check their hands for signs of nerve compression.

title: Tenshi Harness
description: In this shibari tutorial, Tifereth teaches her chest-free Tenshi Harness together with her models Irkalla, Fuoco and Mickael.
about:
GO TO TENSHI HARNESS GUIDE

In this shibari tutorial, Tifereth teaches her chest-free Tenshi Harness together with her models Irkalla, Fuoco and Mickael.

Tifereth first developed the Tenshi Harness back in 2016, and since then it’s taken off as a versatile upper body harness that avoids some of the sustainability challenges associated with harnesses that incorporate ropes across the chest. This course will teach you everything you need to know about the Tenshi: from how it was developed and got its angel-inspired name to harness construction, safety, and how to tailor it to different body types, as well as how to attach uplines and use it in space.

The first part of the course offers a step-by-step demonstration on how to build the Tenshi, with important considerations for tensioning as well as tips for rope bottoms on how to help (or, rather, not help) to ensure correct rope placement.

The ‘Tenshi Safety’ video explores considerations for risk-reduction as you tie, with special attention given to movement, body manipulation, tension and line placement, and how they may impact the nerves of the upper and lower arms.

In the ‘Tailoring the Tenshi’, Tifereth demonstrates subtle but important adjustments for tweaking the tie to better suit different anatomies and levels of mobility.

Finally, the ‘Suspension Lines’ video explores where and how to attach suspension lines to the Tenshi for more experienced practitioners who are ready to take it into the air.

This course is great for expanding your harness repertoire and for learners looking for alternative to TKs. However, please keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from these classes and only use this harness in suspension if that is already a part of your rope practice.
