title: Geeking About The TK
description: In this shibari tutorial, Gorgone will be going in-depth on a foundational shibari tie – namely, the TK (takate kote) or box-tie.
about:
In this rope bondage tutorial, Gorgone will be going in-depth on a foundational shibari tie with their model Hongor – namely, the TK (takate kote) or box-tie.

As Gorgone explains, the TK is one harness that arguably involves almost all of the important ‘building blocks’ used in rope bondage, including things like tension, body mechanics, different frictions, nerve and placement safety – all thoughts and strategies that improve bondage skills.

The first class of this course is focused on the ‘theory’ of TKs. There are many different types of TKs and despite similarities across them, a one-size-fits-all approach does not apply. In this class, Gorgone will discuss variations in terms of style, priorities, needs, body types and more, summarizing everything useful they’ve learned in more than a decade of using this type of tie.

The second class in the course offers a practical positional study dedicated to skills and knowledge that are essential long before you even begin to place your ropes. With a focus primarily on body manipulation and body awareness, this class is key to understanding how to create a comfortable, safe and sustainable TK.

The third class offers a comprehensive demonstration of tying the TK, considerations that will come up as you tie as well as common mistakes people make when tying TKs and how to avoid them. Finally, Gorgone explores the pros and cons of adding a third rope to your TKs.

This class is suitable from beginner level up, though please only apply to your practice as far as your skill set will allow.
safety: This is designated a level 3 harness course because it contains relatively high complexity, requires excellent tension, and/or is more strenuous to be tied in. If you’re newer to studying suspendable harnesses, consider starting with level 2 harnesses. As rope crosses the arms in this course, we suggest the person being tied be familiar with how to check their hands for signs of nerve compression.
equipment: At least two hanks of rope

title: Advanced Predicaments
description: In this course, Fred teaches two advanced predicament ties and shares detailed explanations about balance, body mechanics, and build-up.
about:
In this course, Fred Hatt teaches two advanced predicament ties with his model Briki. In both classes, he shares detailed explanations about balance, body mechanics and build-up (of ties and endorphins) for both riggers and rope bottoms. The ties taught in this course both require a suspension point.

Predicaments are Fred's favourite form of rope play. Endurance, impossible choices, and playing with his bottom’s headspace are the key ingredients in the equation. These ties can be difficult to achieve without good knowledge of the body and in this form of play rigger and model are working ‘against’ each other rather that with each other, so it becomes important to recognise ways in which the model can ‘cheat’ while always paying extreme attention to detail and body cues to keep the bottom safe.

In the first class, Fred teaches a simple form of his signature 'Pyramid Tie'. This tie is a perfect entry point to Predicament Play, using only simple knots while conveying clearly the concept of threat vs effort in a tie.

In the second class, Fred teaches the 'Misery Tie' a more advanced and challenging predicament form. At the end of the class, Fred and Briki share some feedback and extra information about their experience playing with this tie.

Expect hair ties, crotch ropes and burning muscles... This course is not for the faint of heart!

title: Intentional Third Rope
description: In this shibari course, hua hua teaches a series of Intentional Third Ropes for TKs with her models Dantianshi and Kahrin.
about:
In this shibari course, hua hua teaches a series of Intentional Third Ropes for TKs with her models Dantianshi and Kahrin.

Why use a third rope in your TKs? As hua hua explains in the first part of this multi-class series, third ropes in shibari are a versatile and often valuable addition to your TK pattern, with various options to explore based on the type of sensation, function or play you want to add to your tie. In other words, determine your needs and intentions and you’ll likely be able to add a third rope approach to match. Applicable to both stemmed and stemless TKs, third ropes can reinforce or add stability to the structure in suspensions, can offer a deeper sense of restriction, or can be included for aesthetic reasons. After diving into the reasons why you might want (or need) to add a third rope, hua hua goes deeper into the how with three examples that you can add to your own favorite TKs, detailing how to tie them as well as the advantages of each.

In the Tasuki class, hua hua teaches a third rope pattern that places rope just inside of and over the shoulders for a chest-opening effect. Demonstrated on both a stemless TK and a stemmed TK, she shares insights into how the Tasuki pattern can offer functional support in stemmed versions, or alternatively, create more of a decorative element in stemless TKs. hua hua also offers tips on how to make it either more or less challenging for the bottom, depending – of course – on your intention.

In the X-shape class, hua hua teaches two versions of a third rope pattern that creates a cross-shape over the chest: one for stemless TKs and one for stemmed TKs. Much like the Tasuki, the X-shape can serve an aesthetic and a functional purpose but, due to the wraps that pass very close to the neck, has some important risk considerations too. An effective tool for amping up sensations of compression and choking, this pattern is best utilized with prior consideration and only when you’ve agreed that you intentionally want to incorporate breath play elements into your tying.

In the V-shape class, hua hua shares both a stemmed and stemless version of her favorite third rope pattern. Constructed to create a V-shape and stem at the front of the harness, this variation creates another supportive structure with which to play – whether that’s breath play, using it to help create more lift in a face-up suspension or for attaching to another part of the body depends entirely on your scene and your intentions.

This course is ideal for riggers who are starting to feel comfortable with tying harnesses and want to bring more intentionality into that area of their practice. While these third rope examples can add important structural support during suspensions, please keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from these classes and only use these harnesses in suspension if that is already a part of your rope practice. Bottoms should be comfortable maintaining a box-tie/TK position.

* Captions available for this series: English
safety: This is a harness course that contains high complexity, requires excellent tension, and is more strenuous to be tied in. As rope crosses the arms and can be used to intensify the tie, we suggest the person being tied be familiar with hand checks and have good communication skills and body awareness.
equipment: At least three hanks of rope

title: Bottom Talk: Bamboo and Booty Basket Sequence
description: In this voice-over discussion, Cutebutdeadly shares her experience of being tied in Kissmedeadlydoll’s Bamboo and Booty Basket Sequence.
about:
In this voice-over discussion, Cutebutdeadly shares her experience of being tied in Kissmedeadlydoll’s Bamboo and Booty Basket Sequence.

Each tie comes with its own unique challenges as well as moments of relief or heightened intensity, and our Bottom Talk classes are all about shifting the focus from how to tie certain shapes or sequences to how to receive them. During this insightful commentary, Cutebutdeadly explains what she likes about incorporating bamboo into a suspension, how she approaches the predicament element of certain positions (who knew shaking is more of a no-no than not breathing for her?), and how she’s learned to recognize her limits in rope.

As an advanced suspension sequence full of challenging transitions (and with a length of bamboo thrown in just to up the ante), there’s no disputing the rope skills need to tie Doll’s Bamboo and Booty Basket Sequence. But what’s it like from a bottom’s perspective, to be on the other side of the rope being moved and manipulated through this tie? Bottoms will want to listen to this voice over to compare and contrast their own experiences with Cutebutdeadly's, not because one experience is right or wrong, but because hearing how other bottoms manage intense sensations is a fundamental part of learning to bottom. Riggers will gain valuable insights from hearing another perspective on what this sequence can or should feel like!

This class is suitable for all levels to gain a bottom-centric perspective on a challenging sequence with valuable advice that can be incorporated at every level of your bottoming practice. However, please keep your experience level in mind before you try this one yourself – this suspension is for bottoms who are confident in their communication, body awareness and ability to process difficult sensations.

title: Agura Transition Sequence
description: In this shibari tutorial, Bänana teaches an Agura Transition Sequence with her model Marion.‌
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Bänana teaches an Agura Transition Sequence with her model Marion.‌

It’s a common misconception to think that suspension transition sequences have to be fast-moving, dynamic and energetic, which – if you prefer a slower, more deliberate pace when tying – can make them feel quite daunting. This, Bänana explains, was her own concern, until she started trying more transition sequences and discovered that taking a calmer, less hurried and more meticulous approach can be a good thing! Using a three-rope Agura Tie and a three-rope TK, Bänana demonstrates a shibari suspension sequence that progresses from an inverted torsion to a gyaku ebi position, before being inverted and compacted for a final ebi shape.

‌As Bänana emphasizes in the Conclusion video, it’s not about recreating the tie exactly step by step but rather about always thinking about the next step or position. It’s important to be precise, she explains, with a reminder that feedback from the person being tied can be very valuable tool for refining your tying in these challenging yet rewarding sequences.

This class is suitable for advanced practitioners with ample suspension experience recommended for both rigger and model. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own rope practice.‌

title: Positional Study For Futomomo
description: In this shibari class, Fuoco discusses best practices for labbing futomomos with her model Enna.
about:
In this shibari class, Fuoco discusses best practices for labbing futomomos with her model Enna.

Discovering what works for you and your body as a rope bottom and being able to make small but impactful modifications together with your rigger is key to confident and comfortable rope labbing sessions.

This class explores the positional adjustments that models or riggers can make in order to make a tie feel either more easily endurable or – should you want a challenge – more strenuous, focusing specifically on futomomos and creating sustainable single-point inversions in these calf-to-thigh harnesses.

Additionally, Fuoco shares her tips and tricks for how to approach loading the body in the air so as to allow the bottom to acclimate to the harness before dialing up the intensity with a single-point suspension.

This class is intended for intermediate to advanced levels and should only be applied to your practice if you already have some suspension experience. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own practice.

title: Physical Rope: Partials
description: In this shibari class, Tifereth explores techniques for physical rope in partial suspensions with her model Irkalla.
about:
In this shibari class, Tifereth explores techniques for physical rope in partial suspensions with her model Irkalla.

Building on the elements of using both your rope and your body for pushing, pulling and stretching as taught in Tifereth’s ‘Physical Rope: Ground’ class, the second part of this series adds an extra dynamic to your physical rope toolbox: gravity.

The first drill, ‘Playing With Gravity’, is designed to help you find flow and movement in a partial suspension starting out with some simple wrist cuffs. As Tifereth explains, you should stick to this drill for as long as you need to get a feel for this dynamic and connective way of tying. For the person being tied, this is also an opportunity to practice active participation, communication and awareness of how you hold yourself in these types of ties.

The second drill, ‘Making Connections’, expands on the skills you practiced in the first, adding more rope and getting deeper into this style of rope with Tifereth demonstrating where you might find opportunities as well as how to playfully exploit them. Be prepared to feel awkward at first, she says. The rope is simple – wraps and single-columns – but the technique is what comes with time and practice. The more you practice the deeper mechanics of body manipulation play, the more confident you’ll become. For Tifereth and Irkalla, this hands-on type of tying is one of their favorite ways to connect, allowing their dynamic to shine.

This class requires some experience with partial suspensions and tying suspension lines. To explore play with these techniques for any level of experience, check out the Physical Rope: Ground’ class.

This is the second of three ‘Physical Rope’ focused courses led by Tifereth. Keep an eye out for ‘Physical Rope: Suspension’ – coming soon!

title: Self-Tying The Chest
description: In this series of tutorials, Anna Bones will teach various chest ties suitable for self-tying with her model… herself!
about:
In this series of tutorials, Anna Bones will teach various chest ties suitable for self-tying with her model… herself!

While many Shibari Study harnesses can be adapted for self-tying, this four-part course is our first dedicated content focused specifically on self-tying and should give solo rope practitioners a far more nuanced insight as well as specialized tips and tricks for rope bondage without a partner.

The first video eases into self-tying with a super easy pattern that keeps all the knots in the front of the tie. The second is little more challenging, with the knots in the back, while the third class steps things up again with extra decorative elements. The last video is the final boss and will challenge budding self-tyers with knots in the back as well as aesthetic additions.

We encourage all Shibari Study students, whether beginners or experienced in tying on others, to challenge yourself to this super fun series and perhaps even begin a new self-tying journey!

In this rope bondage tutorial, Gigi teaches a modified version of the Mermaid Tie on their model Cait.

As Gigi explains, this tie is wonderfully suited to inversions in suspension, creating a beautiful backbend while also offering plenty of support. This version of the Mermaid Tie takes that sustainability for the model a step further, as is detailed in the first video, with additional support built into the back and kannukis to stabilize the lines and prevent them from sliding in suspensions.

The second part of this shibari class focuses on suspension lines and how best to load the tie to take it from floor-play to flying. This versatile lower body tie can be paired with many types of chest harness, with Gigi offering suggestions of some of their favorite ties to use together with it.

In this rope bondage tutorial, Ropunawa teaches the Half Basket Tie with his model Freya.

The Basket Tie is a popular and classic shape that has taken Shibari Study students all the way from basic beginner ties to supportive suspensions and simple-yet-challenging inversions. As taught by Ropunawa, the Half Basket offers a twist on the familiar full version, only capturing one leg to the waist. Because the Half Basket is less stable than its full counterpart, it’s important to understand the risks involved, which Ropunawa details in this class. As always, please only attempt suspending from this tie if you have prior experience with suspensions.

title: Carabiner Theory
description: In this shibari class, Hajime Kinoko discusses why carabiners are an essential piece of equipment in his rope kit.
about:
In this shibari class, Hajime Kinoko discusses why carabiners are an essential piece of equipment in his rope kit.

By the time your rope practice has progressed to the point of beginning to explore partial or full suspensions, you’ll be faced with different hardware options for your suspension point. While tying on rings and bamboo may be most popular, in this shibari theory class, Kinoko explains why, more than 24 years since he started tying, he remains a lifelong carabiner fan. From upline management, versatility and creative possibilities to creating a particular headspace and sense of rhythm, Kinoko dives deep into his favorite things about this sometimes-underutilized piece of bondage gear.

This class is aimed at anyone already practicing partial and/or full suspensions. Please keep your own skill set in mind and only use the techniques taught in this class if they feel suitable and applicable for your practice. And because not all carabiners are created equal, it’s essential that you only use load-rated carabiners for rope. Always ensure the safety of your gear before you play.

title: Rope As A Breath Play Tool
description: In this rope bondage course, Docvale discusses how to begin exploring breath play in ropes with his model Bänana.
about:
In this rope bondage course, Docvale discusses how to begin exploring breath play in ropes with his model Bänana.

For those starting out in shibari, there may be a tendency to think of breath play as involving choking, tying the neck or gags. However, as Docvale and Bänana detail in this six-part course, having an impact on someone’s ability to breathe can be achieved by strategic application of ropes far beyond the obvious. Starting from the basis of a two-rope TK, this course delves into psychology and physiology of breath play with tips and tricks for how to build up from a simple chest harness and increase intensity for (quite literally) breathtaking rope play. Watch the videos in order to learn how to manage and increase the psychological and physical intensity in tandem for safer and more effective breath play:

The ‘Intro' video offers an introduction to breath play and both what to expect from the course as well as what to expect from this type of play.

The second part of the course, ‘Progressivity & Semenawa’, looks at the Semenawa style of shibari and how it lends itself to the physical and emotional intensity of breath play.

In the third video, ‘Psychological Impact – TK2', Docvale and Bänana begin with a simple TK, exploring how even subtle compressions and adjustments to how you tie a TK can already begin to impact breathing.

From a two-rope TK, there are numerous options to build on and play further with the breath, with the fourth video – ‘Neck - Third Rope’ – focusing on how to utilize a third rope to begin experimenting with pressure around the neck.

In the fifth video, ‘Thorax – Fourth Rope’, a fourth rope is added as the focus shifts from constraining thoracic breathing to constraining abdominal breathing, beginning with a tight single-column tie around the waist.

This final video of this breath play course, ‘Belly and Pubis’ looks at tying the belly and below with two options for creating additional compression from below the waist.

Breath play is a powerful type of edge play, so it’s essential to keep in mind that while elements of this course may be applicable to your own practice, restricting a person’s breath can have a profound physical and psychological impact and is never without risk. It is essential for both you and your tying partner to understand these risks before attempting to recreate anything you see in these classes. If your skill set is not suitable to safely attempt this course, feel free to watch the class for inspiration but do not follow along.

This surprising and challenging position can be kept on the floor as a partial suspension or raised to a full suspension. As this is an intense tie meant to be short-lived in the air, it is recommended to use a pulley system in order to lift and lower your model quickly and easily.

The chest harness used by Fred in this demonstration can be replaced by any other comfortable hands-free harness of your choice (e.g. Butterfly Harness or Xana Harness).

title: Choker Tie | Partial Suspension
description: In this bondage tutorial, RopuNawa teaches a partially suspended version of his infamous Choker Tie with his model Freya.
about:
In this bondage tutorial, RopuNawa teaches a partially suspended version of his infamous Choker Tie with his model Freya.

Using just a simple waistline, this class demonstrates how this powerful harness can be incorporated into a partial suspension. While the addition of the suspension line may not be technically complex, this is still a highly demanding tie, which can be stressful for the model both in terms of pain and restricted breathing. With this in mind, RopuNawa also offers essential guidance for what you can play with and what best to avoid in this already challenging position.

The Choker Tie has more than earned its reputation as one of Shibari Study’s most exciting ties, with the new addition of a partial suspension adding even greater intensity. Therefore, we need to stress that this tutorial is only suitable for riggers and models who have extensive prior experience with this type of edge-play. If your skill set is not yet at a level to safely attempt this tie, feel free to watch the class for inspiration but do not follow along.

title: Forward Fold Predicament
description: In this class, Tamandua teaches a standing predicament with his model Alma.
about:
In this class, Tamandua teaches a standing predicament with his model Alma.

This simple yet highly effective predicament offers a delicious mix of pressure and fatigue-based stress. The legs tied into the chest will challenge the bottom's balance and force them to push on their toes to relieve the pressure.

Shifting weight onto the chest harness will relieve the waist but increase the compression of the chest area, rendering breathing more challenging. Vice versa, when shifting weight away from the chest, pressure on the waist will become more painful.

The tie itself is fairly simple to execute and is ideal for those who enjoy playing with "slow burn" positions, giving time to the predicament to build up slowly and become increasingly challenging and pleasurable. You can add accents such as hair rope or gag to add more sensations.

In this class Tam uses a TK (boxtie), but you can feel free to replace it with another chest harness that suits your preference and risk profile better.

In this shibari class, Cait teaches the Woven Heart Harness with their model Gigi.

A modification of Gorgone’s popular Butterfly Harness, the Woven Heart Harness was engineered to prevent the issue of the waist rope sometimes slipping up towards the floating ribs. Functionality and form are beautifully (and quite literally) woven together in this tie, with the eye-catching woven pattern on the front both securing the lines in place and making for more comfortable face-down suspensions with a wider distribution of pressure.

Far from being suitable for face-downs alone, the Woven Heart Harness can be loaded for suspensions from the front, back or side with the second part of the class focusing on where and how to attach your suspension lines.

This shibari class is suitable for all levels from beginner up and models of all body types and flexibility levels. However, please keep your skill set in mind and only attempt to use it for suspensions if you already have some prior experience.

title: Mid-Air Futomomos
description: In this step-by-step shibari tutorial series, Fuoco explores how to gain confidence tying futomomos in mid-air with her model Enna.
about:
In this step-by-step shibari tutorial series, Fuoco explores how to gain confidence tying futomomos in mid-air with her model Enna.

Being able to apply a harness in the middle of a transition scene while your model is suspended is an incredibly useful skill as your rope bondage practice advances. It’s a tool that allows for both longer scenes and better quality of scenes by increasing your options, expanding opportunities for release and relaxation, and – ultimately – helping you develop dynamic tying that will add to the sustainability of your suspension sequences. That is, provided you’re able to do it both well and quickly enough for your model to benefit. However, as you will learn in this two-part futomomo-focused course, tying in the air is very different to tying on the ground and there are numerous variables to consider and account for.

In the first video, Fuoco presents some exercises for tying a futomomo in mid-air with your model in a side suspension. While ungrounded, this is generally a position that doesn’t require a high level of endurance, and gives the option of applying the futomomo to either the top or bottom leg. This class explores how these factors may influence your tying and how to navigate any challenges that arise.

In the second video, you will learn how to practice mid-air futomomos from a more challenging kata-ashi position, which – like the previous drill – comes with its own considerations to manage as you tie.

This class is intended for advanced shibari learners only. These exercises have been developed to help you increase your confidence as you tie in mid-air, so we recommend taking your time to give each drill ample practice and attention. If your skill set is not suitable to safely attempt this course, feel free to watch the class for inspiration but do not follow along.

description: In this tutorial, Lief and Icky teach their Duality Sequence, a rope suspension sequence that “takes a shape and turns it on its head”.
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky teach their Duality Sequence, an advanced rope suspension sequence that “takes a shape and turns it on its head”.

Using a TK, their version of the Booty Basket and a calf-binder, Lief and Icky demonstrate this progressive suspension flow that starts out with a torturous tippy-toes stand-up position and ends in a beautiful, inverted position. During the course of their step-by-step explanation, they explain their decision-making, including tying on a ring rather than bamboo, detail important safety considerations, and offer ideas for other shapes and transitions you can explore. As they explain, there are several variations of this challenging sequence that you can continue and grow with – what’s key is identifying what works for you and what doesn’t, and adapting from there.

This demanding sequence is aimed at riggers and bottoms with plenty of suspension experience. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own rope practice.

title: Lacing Forearm Binder Partial Suspension
description: In this shibari tutorial, Bänana teaches a Lacing Forearm Binder Partial Suspension with her model Marion.
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Bänana teaches a Lacing Forearm Binder Partial Suspension with her model Marion.

Many of the suspensions we see in shibari rely on chest harnesses to bind the arms and upper body. But does that mean we need rope on the chest? Not necessarily. As Bänana demonstrates in this floor-level partial suspension, there are creative ways to bind the hands and suspend the upper body without using any rope on the chest. While tying this way might be beneficial or even necessary for some, excluding the chest also comes with its own challenges, says Bänana, and will require some adjustments and adaptations, particularly in terms of movement and body handling.

In the first class, Bänana demonstrates how to tie the lacing forearm binder, so as to avoid slipping and create a tie stable enough to attach a suspension line. Importantly, she also speaks about blood circulation and nerves, detailing sensations to expect and risk areas to avoid for safer, more risk-aware tying.

In the second class, Bänana combines the lacing forearm binder taught in the first video with a futomomo to begin exploring a partial suspension. Offering advice for how to gradually lift and compact elements of the tie, Bänana explains that once you understand the techniques taught in this class, there are plenty of possibilities for utilizing these two harnesses together for partial suspensions.

This shibari tutorial is suitable for intermediate and advanced students who already have some suspension and upline handling experience. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own rope practice.

title: Drills For Self-Tying Behind Your Back
description: In this shibari tutorial, Kissmedeadlydoll shares a series of exercises and drills for self-tying behind your back with her model… herself!
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Kissmedeadlydoll shares a series of exercises and drills for self-tying behind your back with her model… herself!

As Kissmedeadlydoll explains, knowing how to tie behind your back is helpful if you’re working towards tying harnesses for self-suspensions. However, where you’ve got your eyes to guide you when tying a partner, now you have to rely on your hands, fingers and sense of your rope in space. Tying behind your back requires mobility, dexterity and plenty of practice connecting your brain to your fingers, so this is where drilling key skills until your fingers act as your “eyes” is essential for developing fluidity and confidence. The drills taught in this course will help you learn to feel your way through tying some common frictions and hitches behind your back, including:

1 Half-hitches

2 X-frictions

3 Half Moons and L Frictions

4 Collapsed hangers

Watch and drill each, pausing in between to take as much time as you need to practice each exercise until you’re able to repeat it consistently, smoothly and confidently. This course is perfect for anyone interested in self-tying, as well as anyone looking to improve their tying coordination and proficiency.

title: Positional Breath Play
description: In this shibari course, Docvale discusses how the position of the body in ropes can be used as a breath play tool with his model Bänana.
about:
In this shibari course, Docvale discusses how the position of the body in ropes can be used as a breath play tool with his model Bänana.

If you’re looking for rope play that will quite literally take your breath away, you’ve come to the right course. As a follow-up to ‘Rope As A Breath Play Tool’, the French instructors continue to delve into breath restriction as an element of rope scenes, focusing on three positions that use compression or alignment of the body to influence the breathing of the person being tied. The classes also explore tips and tricks for playing with intensity in each of these positions, as well as offering feedback from Bänana regarding her experience in the ties.

In the ‘Arch’ video, Docvale uses the example of a floor-based Gyaku Ebi or hog tie to illustrate how an arched position puts pressure on key parts of the respiratory system, while the compression of gravity against the ground and the tie itself prevents the rib cage from fully expanding.

In the ‘Torsion’ video, Docvale uses a semi-suspended ‘mermaid’ position to discuss the role of twisting the body at the waist as a means for influencing the breath with variations for creating more or less pressure.

In the ‘Compacted Position’ video, Docvale offers some ideas for how to use compression and compaction – in this case, starting with a loaded TK as a basis for beginning to wrap the knees towards the chest.

Breath play is a powerful type of edge play, so it’s essential to keep in mind that while elements of this course may be applicable to your own practice, restricting a person’s breath can have a profound physical and psychological impact and is never without risk. It is essential for both you and your tying partner to understand these risks before attempting to recreate anything you see in these classes. If your skill set is not suitable to safely attempt this course, feel free to watch the class for inspiration but do not follow along.

In this bondage tutorial, Ropunawa teaches a fully suspended version of his intense Choker Tie with his model Freya.

Rounding off his Choker Tie-based series of classes, Ropunawa demonstrates how the powerful tie can be incorporated into a visually dramatic suspension. Though the shape looks drastic, much of its weight is spread between the Futomomo and waist line, making it surprisingly comfortable for models who like suspending off of these types of ties. However, it’s not without its technical demands: starting on the ground, it’s lifted almost all the way with a Futomomo, meaning you need to be aware of how to lift heavy parts of the body and best practice for suspension lines.

We’ve been building up to this breathtaking inversion with Ropunawa’s earlier Choker Tie classes – and for good reason. The Choker Tie is a challenge on its own, and the addition of suspension lines brings with it a new level of complexity that requires plenty of experience with both suspensions and this type of edge-play. title: Self-Suspension Safety Talk
description: In this shibari class, KissmedeadlyDoll sits down for some self-suspension safety real talk aimed at solo rope practitioners.
about:
In this shibari class, KissmedeadlyDoll sits down for some self-suspension safety real talk aimed at solo rope practitioners.

Easy there, self-tyer! Before you get yourself into a bind that you can’t get out of, put your ropes aside and get real with KissmedeadlyDoll as she dives deep into safety for self-suspension. As a self-tyer and self-suspender with more than a decade’s experience, Doll has learned a few tricks along the way… and fucked up a couple of times too. In this shibari safety lecture, she shares everything she knows – and everything she wishes she’d known – to help make your first forays into self-suspending safer, smoother and more confident. From planning and managing risk to emergency back-up plans, this is essential viewing for everyone who’s their own rigger and model all rolled up into one.

This class is suitable for all levels, though the techniques discussed in this class are aimed at self-tying practitioners who are already starting to explore suspensions. As KissmedeadlyDoll explains, being cognizant of “when are you ready to self-suspend?” is part of safer self-suspension, so please be mindful of your own skill set as you decide if you’re ready to elevate your bondage practice.

title: Kinoko's Forearm Binder
description: This online tutorial by Hajime Kinoko shows how to tie his Forearm Binder.
about:
In this class, Hajime Kinoko teaches his Forearm Binder with his model Maya Homerton.

Equal parts bold and intricate, straightforward and complex, when used on its own, this snug structure’s impressive aesthetic belies just how easy it is to tie – in fact, it’s perfect for Shibari beginners. It can also offer an exciting challenge to more practiced students wanting to use it for suspension.

This forearm binder works well for vertical suspensions with most of the load on the lower body and care should be taken not to create too much load on the hands. We recommend using it paired with our Hip Loader (or a hip-loaded variation of the Butterfly Harness) to create stunning and comfortable vertical suspensions that ask nothing more of the bottom’s hands and arms than to look beautiful!

title: Performance with Ms Reemah and Anansi (FREE)
description: Ms Reemah and Anansi share a captivating tying session that showcases the collaborative side of a challenging scene.
about:
In this shibari performance, Ms Reemah and Anansi share a captivating tying session that showcases the collaborative side of a challenging scene.

It’s said that you never have the same experience in rope twice, and there’s no better example of this maxim than Ms Reemah and Anansi’s mesmerizing suspension performance. Strenuous from the get-go with a gag and face rope, the performance video instantly demonstrates the essential softer side of “mean” rope: checking in as praxis, making adjustments as needed, and problem-solving on the fly. The result is a scene as characterized by care and collaboration as it is by intense shapes and transitions (and yes, just a little evil waist rope too).

The performance is followed by an insightful debrief discussion between the tying partners discussing their experiences of the session. Perhaps their joke “accidentally on purpose” sums it up best: by allowing space for exploration, intention and course correcting, even approaching play from a familiar starting point can result in intriguing new outcomes.

This performance is suitable for all to watch and enjoy. As always, remain mindful of your own skill set and allow this class to inspire you accordingly.

title: Mayfly TK
description: In this class, Gestalta teaches two versions of their Mayfly TK.
about:
In this class, Gestalta teaches two versions of their Mayfly TK with their model Aleks.

Both variations offer the basic functionality of a traditional TK but with an interesting twist. By keeping the arms down at the side of the body instead of in the usual behind-the-back 'box-tie' position of a standard TK, the stress of internal rotation is taken out of the shoulders, making for a more comfortable and sustainable tie.

In suspension, this harness leaves the arms draped around the body for a poetic and less traditional aesthetic. It’s an ideal option for bottoms who are comfortable with pressure on their arms but have limited flexibility in their shoulders.

The 'Original' version of the tie is the more structured of the two and is recommended for transitions or extended time periods.

Where the first variation offers stability and practicality, the second delivers the drama, with a dynamic 'exploding' take on the harness that comes off easily in the air, making it a thrilling tie for both performance and play. You can see it used in action in the Mayfly Session.

title: Creating Imbalance In Floor Play
description: In this shibari course, Docvale and Bänana discuss how the use of imbalance in ropes can create an element of surprise and intensity.
about:
In this shibari course, Docvale and Bänana discuss how the intentional use of imbalance in ropes can create an element of surprise and intensity.

You need to have good understanding of how to create and control balance in order to start playing with intentionally disrupting it, says Docvale (check out the ‘Creating Balance’ course as a starting point). While creating balance can refine your communication in ropes, mindfully exploring imbalance can be a playful way to create new physical and psychological challenges, even in floor play.

In the first tutorial, the pair use the example of forearm lacing to begin introducing this type of movement manipulation. This particular harness is a useful tool to begin exploring how the quality of your communication translates to ease of play. As explained by Docvale, you want to invite movement rather than force it in order to better help the person being tied relax into the ropes.

In the second tutorial, a Strappado is used to further demonstrate how creating imbalance can be an effective and highly visceral tool for more psychological rope play. During the class, Docvale offers various options for turning up the intensity by further compressing the body to make maintaining balance even trickier.

Finally, in the third tutorial, Docvale demonstrates how this type of play can be used in a cross-legged ebi position. While this position may seem highly stable, it only takes some compacting and a little manipulating the body to create total imbalance even here.

This course is suitable for all levels, although it’s recommended that you get comfortable with the ‘Creating Balance’ series first, before you begin playing with imbalance.

In this rope bondage tutorial, Cait teaches their Diamond Back Hip Harness on their model Gigi.

Inspired by Anna Bones and Fred Hatt’s ‘Bones and Rope’ hip harness, Cait created this hip harness to give a little extra back support to larger bodied models. Where more minimalistic hip harness may not provide enough support, the Diamond Back Hip Harness is designed to be both comfortable and aesthetic, with a waist rope, thigh wraps and extra rope over the backside to make it supportive and sustainable for bigger models in suspensions.

In the first video, Cait demonstrates how to tie the harness itself, sharing their tips and tricks for controlling tension and placement when tying bigger bodied people.

In the second video, they demonstrate how to attach suspension lines for the harness, with important advice on how to spread the load to make the most of the harness’s supportive structure.

This shibari tutorial is suitable for intermediate students and models of all body types and flexibility levels. Please keep your skill set in mind and only attempt suspensions if you already have some experience.

title: Self-Suspension Uplines And The Body
description: In this self-tying shibari class, Kissmedeadlydoll explores Self-Suspension Uplines and the Body with her model… herself!
about:
In this self-tying shibari class, Kissmedeadlydoll explores Self-Suspension Uplines and the Body with her model… herself! In this course, you’ll learn how both uplines and your own body can be important tools for a creative and dynamic self-suspension practice.

After more than a decade of self-tying and self-suspending, Kissmedeadlydoll has learnt a thing or two about how to do-it-yourself in ropes. From active bottoming through new shapes, creative transitions into inversions, and even a nifty trick that’ll turn a removable thigh cuff into a new hard point, this course is all about making your uplines and your body work for you in self-suspensions.

This self-suspension course is divided into five parts, beginning with an introduction and lecture, before moving on to three classes that demonstrate different skills and options available to self-tyers in practice. Finally, Kissmedeadlydoll combines all the skills demonstrated in the previous videos to show how torsions, rotations, transitions from face-up to face-down, and more can be accessible to self-suspenders with clever upline and body involvement.

This course is aimed at self-tyers who already have some suspension experience. As Kissmedeadlydoll explains, spend some time planning your suspensions, deciding where you want to go and mapping out your journey to get there. Allow this course to inspire and guide you as far as your skill set will allow.

title: Study On Falling
description: In this shibari tutorial, Gorgone will be teaching their ‘Study on Falling’ suspension sequence with their model Vivian.
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Gorgone will be teaching their ‘Study on Falling’ suspension sequence with their model Vivian.

One of Gorgone’s favorite suspension sequences, they have performed it extensively over the years and now, for the first time ever, will be teaching it on Shibari Study.

Gorgone designed this sequence as a way to surrender to the experience of extreme vulnerability, letting go and “falling” into the rope. As they explain in the class intro, while this may not be too complicated to tie for the rigger, it is a very intense sequence for the person being tied and carries a higher risk profile due to the last position in particular – a single-point waist rope suspension dropping into a fairly extreme backbend shape. As such, it’s essential to go through it slowly, with confidence and with no resistance in the body of the person being tied.

As a suspension sequence that is both physically demanding and at-times psychologically challenging, the class offers insights into ways in which to make it more manageable for the person being tied, such as starting out with a hands-free chest harness to allow the model more control, as well as Gorgone’s tips for how to reassure yourself and your tying partner as you move through this exquisite and powerful progression. They also offer essential advice for warming up beforehand and getting accustomed to the sensation of dropping into the single waist line.

This class is aimed at advanced students with plenty of suspension experience only. Please watch the videos in full, familiarize yourself with the sequence and do not push yourself if you feel any uncertainty or resistance, particularly going into the last position.
safety: This is a level 4 course that requires significant previous suspension experience from both the person tying and the person being tied. We always suggest learning new sequences with the support of a spotter or with the supervision of a qualified instructor.
equipment: At least six hanks of rope

The forearms are tightly bound to the main structure but not locked into the chest, allowing for more mobility and possibilities to vary the aesthetics and sensations of your suspension. title: Ebi-Zeme Variation
description: In this class, Gestalta teaches a floor-based variation of Agura & Ebi Shibari with their model Aleks.
about:
In this class, Gestalta teaches a floor-based variation of Agura & Ebi Shibari with their model Aleks.

Modern Shibari refers to any crossed-leg sitting position as Agura Shibari. If the upper body is tied and forced close to the open legs, it is called Ebi Shibari (shrimp tie) or Ebi Seme (shrimp torment). The body being bent forward and the knees widely spread, the position resembles the body and tail of a prawn or shrimp.

Gestalta revisits this classic position inspired by an ancient method of torture, ebi-zeme (海老責め).

If kept for a long period of time, this position will heavily restrict the breathing and generate strong blood flow restrictions creating a burning sensation throughout the entire body. The increased stress created by the variations of leg position she explains and demonstrates in this class will make the effect significantly more immediate and efficient on flexible models.

title: Masterclass: Nerve Compression Management (Free)
description: In this voice-over lecture, Ms Reemah and Anansi are in conversation with Fuoco, discussing nerve compression management in shibari.
about:
In this voice-over lecture, Ms. Reemah and Anansi are in conversation with Fuoco, discussing nerve compression management in shibari, accompanied by a real-time example of how they addressed it during a tie.

Nerve compression is one of the most common risks in shibari and as your practice progresses to include more challenging ties and suspensions, it’s not so much a question of ‘if’ rather than ‘when’. That ‘when’ can range from every scenario, from labbing to performances to, yes, on set for a Shibari Study production. While things may not always go according to plan in ropes, what is essential is having a strategy for addressing and managing complications such as nerve compression when they do occur – here, Ms Reemah and her model Anansi demonstrate a masterclass in exactly that.

This course provides a thorough example of what it looks like when nerve issues do occur during a tie. Remember that rope is highly personal and what feels like an acceptable risk to some may not be an acceptable risk to others, and how some people mitigate or manage risks may not be an option in every situation or tying dynamic. The intention of this class is not to provide an example that must be imitated exactly but, rather, to show how it can be done. Throughout the conversation, Ms Reemah and Anansi explore what effective communication can look like when problems arise, discuss the various adjustments they tried to troubleshoot the issue, and reflect on how they managed the moment together.

This class is appropriate for all levels as an example of what effective action can look like in the case of nerve compression in ropes. While this can inspire you, always let your own context, experience and risk-profile guide you to take the action most appropriate for you.

In this shibari class, Gorgone will teach you their Flying Lotus vertical suspension with their model Hongor.

Minimalistic, magical and, above all else, easy to execute, the Flying Lotus is a great suspension to practice collaborative tying. By lifting the model into a vertical cross-legged position in the air, the person being tied is comfortably able to take control of their own balance, making for a tie that feels more synergistic and relaxed for both model and rigger alike. title: Creating Balance
description: In this shibari series, Docvale and Bänana discuss the influence of technique in rope and creating better balance in your shibari practice.
about:
In this Shibari tutorial, Docvale and Bänana discuss the influence of technique in rope, focusing on three areas where mindfully adjusting your approach can create better balance in your shibari practice.

As soon as you need to use force as a rigger, says Docvale, there’s probably a trick you’re missing that could make it simpler. Good riggers, he says, are lazy – they understand that the less complicated you make things and the less you force, the easier it will be to tie. This course is intended to help you bring intentionality into aspects of your rope practice where it’s easy to develop bad habits, and while the lessons covered in these classes may be tricky to implement at first, they will have a positive impact on your practice in the long run.

The first class focuses on the position and posture of rigger. In this tutorial, Docvale will discuss the pros and cons of different positions in terms of exertion, how dynamic they are, the level of stability they offer, and how impactful they are or what they communicate to the person being tied.

The second part of this course looks at tips and tricks for better rope handling, as this is an aspect of your practice that can both generate balance as well as create imbalance, particularly in partial and full suspensions. We all tie in a sequential way, says Docvale, but it’s good rope handling that gives our tying a sense of fluidity.

The final two classes focus on body manipulation with essential advice for how to use less force for greater results both when the person being tied is seated as well as when they are standing up. In these classes, Docvale discusses how too much superfluous movement can lead to imbalance and mixed messages while clear and intentional movement can effectively communicate intent and make for a better bondage practice.

This course is suitable for all levels and is recommended for anyone looking to refine the way they communicate through their tying.

This tie can be easily modified to suit different bodies or aesthetics, however it can be quite unpredictable in the air and shouldn't be suspended without special attention and care for the possibility of nerve compression or slippage of the wraps over the shoulders.

title: Ankle Ties
description: In this shibari tutorial, Gorgone teaches the ins and outs of ankle ties.
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Gorgone teaches the ins and outs of ankle ties, from important considerations to get started all the way to a single ankle suspension.

Ankles are extremely delicate, meaning tying them improperly can fast become painful to the point of untying. In this series of ankle tie-focused classes, Gorgone covers techniques and applications that can make these sometimes-intimidating ties easier, safer and more sustainable.

The first class of this four-part series lays the groundwork for further exploring loading the ankles with useful advice for figuring out where pressure on the ankle may be less or more tolerable based on the anatomy of the person being tied.

In the second class, Gorgone details important preparations and adjustments that can be made before loading the tie.

The third-class is a more bottom-focused exploration of ankle ties, and looks at how the person being tied can actively influence their comfort in these ties and reduce pressure on this sensitive part of the body.

Finally, using all the information shared in the first three classes, the fourth class demonstrates a more sustainable, more beautiful and more comfortable single ankle suspension. (Please note: this suspension is categorically not recommended for self-suspension – only try inversions such as this with someone on hand to assist.)

While aspects of this course may be applicable from an intermediate level on, the single-ankle suspension is recommended for advanced practitioners with plenty of suspension experience only. Please always exercise caution when attempting this tie.

title: Reverse Prayer Tie
description: In this shibari class, Ropunawa teaches his take on the Reverse Prayer Tie with his model Freya.
about:
In this shibari class, Ropunawa teaches his take on the Reverse Prayer Tie with his model Freya.

Ropunawa’s latest class is a structural-but-fun challenge for both rigger and model alike. With hands tied in a ‘prayer’ position behind the back, the Reverse Prayer Tie is a visually striking harness that relies as much on the shoulder flexibility of the person being tied as it relies on the skill of the person doing the tying. An essential check to do before beginning is to see if the model’s hands comfortably fit into the space between their shoulder – with that confirmed, you can go ahead and get started with this rewarding tie.

This tie is suitable for all students from intermediate level up, however, it is not suitable for every model. Only attempt to do it if their flexibility allows for it.

title: Tying Bigger Bodies
description: In this four-part rope bondage tutorial series, tying partners Cait and Gigi discuss rope for bigger bodies.
about:
In this four-part rope bondage tutorial series, tying partners Cait and Gigi discuss rope for bigger bodies.

There is very little representation of bigger bodies in bondage and, as a result, many misconceptions and negative stereotypes around tying bigger bodies. This course is designed to emphasize the fact that every body is unique and that rope is adaptable. As Cait and Gigi explain, it’s about knowing how to tie the person you intend to tie, about partnership (being able to communicate openly and being receptive to feedback) and about being able to modify ties to work for you.

In the intro video, Cait and Gigi go over some all-important safety considerations to take into account before starting with the rest of the course.

The next videos cover the topic of harness stability and comfort, with useful advice on how to approach tension and rope placement when tying bigger models, including a useful exercise you can incorporate into your rope practice for finding the best tension and placements in your ties.

Finally, Cait and Gigi offer their tips and tricks for getting bigger bodies into the air in suspensions.

While elements of this video series for tying bigger bodies can be beneficial for every level and any practice, please keep your skill set in mind and only attempt the suspension part of the course if you already have some prior experience.

description: In this shibari series, Tamandua teaches a suspension and inversion focused on the leg tie (Futomomo).
about:
In this series, Tamandua will teach a suspension and inversion focused on the leg-tie (or futomomo) with his model Elio.

In two shibari classes aimed at more experienced riggers, Tamandua shows how a rope bondage fundamental, the futomomo or leg tie, can be incorporated into more demanding and intense scenes.

The tie, which involves securing the thigh to the calf, is often one of the first that rope bondage students learn. In these tutorials, this bondage basic is upgraded for a side suspension starting from standing and then for a dramatic progression into an inversion from the floor. Included, too, is a feedback session from Elio detailing his experiences in these challenging ties.

This series is suitable only for students experienced with suspensions and should not be attempted by anyone still in the early stages of elevating their rope play from the ground.

In this class Gorgone and her model Xana demonstrate a simple partial suspension using the Xana Harness and Diamond Leg Tie.

It is also a wonderful way to explore suspension sensations in a more relaxed, playful or intimate way, rather than focusing on complicated, stressful and challenging techniques.

title: Yoko Tsuri Study
description: This series by Gestalta teaches and explains different variations of the Yoko Tsuri, a type of side suspension.
about:
In this course, Gestalta demonstrates and explains different variations of Yoko-tsuri (side suspension) with their model Aleks.

This class is ideal if you are fairly new to suspension and want to practice a position that is not too challenging for the model and doesn't involve advanced uplines management.

In the first part, they demonstrate a side suspension without hip support, with a few tips on how to get into the position smoothly. They show a few variations and explains the pros and cons of this simple execution of the tie.

In the second part, they demonstrate a side suspension with hip support by using a more supportive tie on the leg as well as adding either a wrap around the hips or a gun slinger harness.

In both classes, they show how the same position can look and feel different by changing the levels of the upper-body in relation to the lower-body and playing around with variations with the remaining leg.

Note that Gestalta is using a TK in the classes, but you can replace it with a hands-free harness to reduce the risk of nerve damage and stress in the shoulders.

title: Active Bottoming For Suspension
description: In this shibari tutorial, Fuoco and her model Gorgone discuss active bottoming in suspensions.
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Fuoco and her model Gorgone discuss active bottoming in suspensions with examples of how more – or less – effort from the person being tied can influence their experience.

For many rope bottoms, learning about active bottoming can be an ‘a-ha!’ moment in their rope education as it’s a practice that enables them to better endure tough ties like suspensions and make their own adjustments to protect their bodies without relying entirely on the rigger. However, as Fuoco and Gorgone – both experienced bottoms and riggers – discuss in this class series, active bottoming is a spectrum that begins with even the subtlest of micro adjustments, and there are even times when passivity may be a better option.

Using three different suspensions as examples, they explore when active bottoming is necessary versus when there’s not much you can do for yourself, and how to tell the difference. As they explain, active bottoming shouldn’t be the thing that’s hardest but that which is most energy efficient. From the rigger perspective, they also demonstrate how observing your bottom’s adjustments can give you clues for how to offer them more support in your ties or make them more challenging…

This shibari tutorial series is suitable for both bottoms and riggers beginning to explore suspensions in rope. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own rope practice.

* Captions available for this series: English
safety: This course introduces bottom-led choices in suspension. It's best practice to familiarize yourself with your body in rope on the floor and through partials before attempting suspension. Once you have built your way up to suspension level, body awareness is a practice that should never end.

title: Active Bottoming
description: In this series Fuoco focuses on movement-in-rope exercises to help understand what "active bottoming" might entail.
about:
In this series you'll find different videos, including movement-in-rope exercises suited to lab-style explorations and physical aftercare, designed to help you:

Understand what "active bottoming" might entail in these common positions of facedown and torsion suspensions.

Develop a sense of when your body is safer/less safe in these positions.

Understand what skills you can develop or utilize, in some situations, to protect the health of your body in these strenuous positions (during and after a session).

Help riggers to have a clearer sense of when a body is in a more or less compromised and challenging position in these types of suspensions.

Help riggers to develop a clearer sense of how to balance stressful positions and put their bottoms into easier or harder variations of these positions.

The point is not that all of your suspension experiences here on out should achieve these sensations of balance and alignment. Rather these are exercises intended to build body awareness. You might find that they help you understand what small adjustments you can ask for to make positions more sustainable or give you a better sense of what micro-adjustments you can make yourself.

For the Facedown Exploration video:

Explore first how you tend to be lifted into the position, and then how it feels to be lifted into the position maintaining a more aligned and engaged open-hip position.

Explore pelvic tilt and low back release, in proper alignment, at various levels, noticing when these subtle movements are more/less accessible to you.

If possible, attempt this on both a ring and bamboo. If bamboo is not available, explore the difference between being very close to the ring (short lines and wide angle) and very close to the floor (long lines and small angle).

Finally, notice if it's possible for you to both be in an aligned hip position and in a balanced facedown shape. Some folks with lots of tightness in this position in their hips might not be able to maintain alignment *and* be lifted into a balanced position (such that the weight of the torso is evenly/comfortably distributed between top and bottom wraps).

Please feel free to use any other harness as an alternative to the TK while practicing these exercises if it is safer and more comfortable for you or your partner.

title: Gender Expanding TK
description: In this rope bondage tutorial, Gorgone teaches adjustment techniques for gender-affirming TKs and chest harnesses with their model Miah.
about:
In this rope bondage tutorial, Gorgone teaches adjustment techniques for gender-affirming TKs and chest harnesses with their model Miah.

Most patterns in shibari are designed for cisgender women, often highlighting the more ‘feminine’ characteristics with emphasis placed on the curves of the body.

However, this does not mean that harnesses or ties can’t be adapted to allow for gender euphoria. In this class, Gorgone details how rope placement in TKs and chest harness in particular are used to accentuate more aspects of the body that are commonly seen as 'feminine', as well as adjustments that can serve to feature deeper gender expansion in the ties.

This class is suitable for all levels, though please only apply to your practice as far as your skill set will allow. Additionally, it serves as an important reminder that shibari is not only for one type of body – it is for every body.

title: Considerations for Self-Tying
description: In this course, Anansi shares a series of self-tying primer tutorials designed to help beginners explore the many benefits of self-tying.
about:
In this shibari course, Anansi shares a series of self-tying primer tutorials designed to help beginners explore the many benefits of self-tying and develop confidence in their practice. Additionally, she offers some ideas for connective exercises for roping others into your self-tying with her models Reemah, Lavender, Enna and Kahrin.

When we think of shibari as a tool for exploring connection and intention, it’s all too easy to forget that not only can these elements be explored without a tying partner but there are real benefits to be derived from tying solo too. This course is built around a series of easy and fun floor-based self-tying exercises that focus on cultivating different facets of self-tying rather than simply recreating certain patterns. As Anansi explains, self-tying can allow practitioners to improve essential rope bottoming skills such as processing various sensations, exploring different types of movement and mindful breathing.

The first two exercises offer starting prompts and intentions to explore both less and more dynamic types of self-tying, so focusing more on stillness or more on movement.

In the next three classes, Anansi demonstrates how self-tying can, in fact, still be a group activity with a series of connective exercises that explore… tying yourself to others!

Finally, the group ties conclude with a casual debrief as the participants discuss what they most enjoyed about these playful takes on connective tying.

This course is suitable for all levels and, with plenty of room for free-styling and adjusting to your own needs, can be adapted for just about any skill set. Remain mindful of your abilities and allow this series to inspire your rope practice accordingly.

about:
In this special shibari session, Bänana discusses how she approaches suspending someone heavier than herself with her model Fred.

Tying well often means knowing how to adapt, says Bänana, and tying someone heavier than yourself shouldn’t be viewed as a problem but simply as another parameter to be considered and adjusted for during the tying session.

During this demonstration and discussion, Bänana explains how pulleys, suspension lines, body handling and mechanics can be managed when suspending someone heavier than you. As she shows throughout the class, even small tweaks can add up to easier and more effective suspensions regardless of the whether the person being tied is heavier than the person doing the tying.

This shibari tutorial is suitable for intermediate and advanced students who already have some suspension experience.

title: Tanuki Tsuri
description: In this class Gestalta teaches a Tanuki Tsuri ("racoon suspension").
about:
In this class, Gestalta teaches a Tanuki Tsuri ("racoon suspension") with their model Olivia.

Minimalistic and challenging on the body, the focus of this advanced tie is on acrobatic prowess and dynamic movement. The transition from face-up (forward fold) to face-down (backbend) is very impressive and may be an interesting exercise for experienced models who enjoy intense proactive bottoming experiences. It will challenge their proprioception and autonomous body coordination in the rope. If you enjoy playing with ties that test both flexibility and stamina, this one is for you! However, as this tie requires a high level of flexibility and resilience from the bottom, it should not be attempted with inexperienced partners.

As Gestalta explains, this tie is intended to be short-lived and should only be suspended with a pulley in order to lift and lower the body swiftly and smoothly, relieving pressure on the wrists as fast and regularly as needed.

We highly recommend negotiating practicing this strenuous tie very carefully and thoroughly to ensure everyone understands that the risks of injury are higher with this suspension. The main risks associated with this tie are nerve compression on the wrists and back/shoulder injury during the transition from the face-up position into a fairly extreme backbend. This class is aimed at advanced riggers and bottoms alike.

title: Connective Uplines
description: In this tutorial, Lief and Icky present some strategies to use suspension uplines to connect more with your partners during rope scenes.
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky present some fun strategies to use suspension uplines to connect more with your partners during rope scenes.

Once you already have plenty of shibari suspension experience, how can you make your scenes as much about connecting with the person in your ropes as it is about tying them well? As Lief and Icky explain, once you already have a good level of technical proficiency when it comes to tying uplines, you can start using those uplines for more connective tying.

This shibari course is divided into five parts, the first video detailing safety consideration for risk mitigation when you start playing with advanced suspension techniques, while the second offers step-by-step instructions for tying Lief and Icky’s favorite bottom lock-off. The next three classes each look at different ways in which your suspension uplines can do double duty, enhancing how you connect with your bottom. These include using extra upline to incorporate hair or mouth rope, combining uplines to create more compression in your suspension shapes and using extra upline to create lift or support in other areas of the tie. Finally, Lief and Icky demonstrate a suspension using all three techniques for a comprehensive example of how they can be used in play.

This shibari class series is aimed at riggers and bottoms who have studied and practiced secure uplines and feel confident enough to start adding a new element of challenge. As Lief and Icky explain, this type of play can add more risk as it adds extra time to your suspensions and may incorporate delicate parts of the body. They recommend beginning to explore these techniques in partial suspensions first. Allow this course to inspire and guide you only as far as your skill set will allow.

title: Infinity Reverse Prayer
description: In this rope bondage tutorial, Gorgone teaches the Infinity Reverse Prayer Tie with their model Hongor.
about:
In this rope bondage tutorial, Gorgone teaches the Infinity Reverse Prayer Tie with their model Hongor.

A challenge for riggers and models alike, this extreme and eye-catching harness is a great tie for more experienced practitioners to play with increased intensity. The first part of the class details exactly how to tie the harness with important safety considerations to keep in mind – please watch through in full before you attempt this tie.

Once you’re well-practiced and ready for the next challenge, the Infinity Reverse Prayer Tie can also be incorporated into suspensions, with the second part of the class focused on where to place your suspension lines as well as where to avoid loading this already-demanding harness.

As Gorgone explains in the class, this harness needs to be tied a lot tighter than a regular TK in order to maintain the position of the hands together between the shoulder blades. Due to the strenuousness of this tie, its risk profile with regards to nerve damage, circulation loss and pain is heightened. Please be mindful that you may have to untie it sooner than you think.

This class is recommended for advanced riggers and models only and should only be attempted with models flexible enough to be in this position.

title: Bottom Led Suspension
description: In this class, Icky and Lief share another one of their labbing-for-better-rope games with a fun Bottom Led Suspension exercise.
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Icky and their tying partner Lief share another one of their labbing-for-better-rope games with a fun Bottom Led Suspension exercise.

Much like just about every other element of shibari, communication takes practice – we drill certain ties and frictions, so why not another essential tying skill: asking for what we need. As Lief and Icky explain, communicating efficiently and effectively about desires and needs while in rope is a critical skill for bottoms but can be difficult when processing challenging feelings or sensations, particularly in suspensions. This engaging exercise allows both the person doing the tying and the person being tied to make decisions about the eventual suspension, creating an intentional space where the only ‘goal’ is being able to express exactly what we need to make our ties feel safer, more sustainable or simply more rewarding.

This exercise is best suited for riggers and rope bottoms with suspension experience, always allowing your own skill set to guide you. If you prefer to play on the floor, feel free to adapt the game to best suit your practice. The goal here is improving your communication and that starts with meeting yourself and your tying partner wherever you’re at in your shibari journey.

* Captions available for this series: English
safety: This is a level 4 course that requires significant previous suspension experience from both the person tying and the person being tied. We always suggest learning new sequences with the support of a spotter or with the supervision of a qualified instructor. As this is improvisational play, both partners should have good communication skills, ability to pivot quickly and body awareness.
equipment: At least six hanks of rope

title: Self-Hug Tie
description: In this step-by-step shibari tutorial, Bänana teaches a Self-Hug partial suspension with her model Fred.
about:
In this step-by-step shibari tutorial, Bänana teaches a Self-Hug partial suspension with her model Fred.

A classic and minimalistic position with the arms wrapped around the backs of the legs, this compact semi-suspension is achieved without the use of a chest harness. Instead, it uses a straightforward Basket Tie and lacing up the lower part of the legs to achieve a playful partial. However, despite not involving too many technical elements, this tie is great for challenging your rope- and body-handling skills. In this class, Bänana demonstrates exactly what you’ll need to keep in mind to achieve the final ‘self-hug’ position as effectively and safely as possible.

This class is suitable for intermediate levels and beyond. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own practice, particularly if you intend to utilize this tie in semi-suspensions.

*Captions available for this class: English
safety: This course utilizes a suspension line to create the final form. Before attempting, you’ll need to first familiarize yourself with safe suspension line technique.
equipment: At least five hanks of rope

title: Safety 301 (Free)
description: A shibari safety and risk-awareness-focused class collection with suspension at its heart.
about:
In this shibari course, fuoco, Kinknamepending and Shakti Bliss present Safety 301, a shibari safety and risk-awareness-focused class collection with suspension at its heart.

What goes up must come down – and this suspension-focused safety collection is aimed at helping you navigate every step of that journey. From the negotiations that happen before you get into the air to situations where you need to come down, and rope-related considerations to nuanced nerve safety, the classes that follow will lay the groundwork for taking your rope practice into the air.

In the first class, fuoco asks, “Is it safe to use jute as an upline?” While this might feel like a loaded question, the answer that follows will help you understand not only the safety factor of your jute rope, but the many variables at play when suspending someone.

In the second class, fuoco’s upline safety theory is practically applied in a suspension demo. The idea? To demonstrate the “everchanging risk landscape” and the way you’ll need to think about the choices you make and their risk and safety implications several steps in advance as you tie.

In the third class, your nerve safety knowledge is expanded for a suspension context as fuoco delves into positional nerve considerations – how changing the position of body in air and different static and dynamic loads exerted on a tie add new layers of complexity to nerve safety.

In the fourth class, Pen and Shakti detail important information to share and factors to consider when negotiating for suspension from both a top and bottom perspective. These include risk profile, skill level, physical and emotional states, communication style, and more.

Finally, Shakti explores the topic of needing to come down. Offering essential advice for both riggers and rope bottoms in these situations, she emphasizes that occasionally requiring an early descent is a normal and valid part of every rope suspension journey!

This shibari safety series is aimed at riggers and bottoms who have moved through or are familiar with the content in Safety 101 and 201 and feel ready to start exploring suspensions. Feel free to come back any time you need to brush up on these topics.

title: Safety 201 (Free)
description: An exploration of important safety knowledge for expanding your rope bondage practice beyond the basics.
about:
In this shibari course, fuoco, Kinknamepending and Shakti Bliss present Safety 201, an exploration of important safety knowledge for expanding your rope bondage practice beyond the basics.

As you begin to tie more elaborate harnesses, add more ropes, or start experimenting with loading your ties, things are becoming not only more challenging, but riskier too. While Safety 101 introduced you to fundamentals for your beginner practice, this series is all about levelling up, making sure you have the risk-awareness to match your developing rope skills.

In the first part of the class, fuoco and Pen share nerve compression safety strategies for both rope bottoms and riggers, including how nerves work, which nerves are most at risk in the hands and arms in upper body harnesses, and the difference between nerve compression and circulation-related sensations.

The next two classes bring fainting into focus. First, Pen explains why someone might lose consciousness in ropes and what to do if someone starts to feel faint in ropes. The next class demos what fainting might look like in a floor-play scene, with practical advice for what to do if it happens with a systematic three-tier approach of protecting life, protecting the body, and recovery.

Finally, Shakti helps you distinguish the difference between “labbing” and “scening”, both ways in which you might be exploring shibari, but often with different contexts, goals and intentions.

This shibari safety series is aimed at riggers and bottoms who have a firm grasp of the basics, are familiar with Safety 101 and are now exploring more complex or risky ties. Feel free to come back any time you need to brush up on these topics.

title: Safety 401 (Free)
description: Expanding your strategies for what to do when things don’t go to plan.
about:
In this shibari course, fuoco, Kinknamepending and Shakti Bliss present Safety 401, a risk-awareness, mitigation and management series that recognizes that more advanced techniques and types of play come with their own unique considerations.

By the time you’re regularly labbing suspensions, experimenting with transitions in the air, and adding often-riskier types of play to your rope scenes, the safety concerns you encounter in your bondage practice may look very different to when you were starting out. The classes that follow are all about expanding your strategies for what to do when things don’t go to plan, as well as exploring how the choices we make ultimately add up to affect our longevity in ropes – both in individual scenes and in the practice as whole.

In the first class, fuoco and Pen level up your fainting safety skill set with a demonstration and discussion on what to do if someone faints in a suspension. As with fainting on the ground, they offer a priority framework of protecting life, protecting the body, and focusing on recovery.

In the second class, Shakti explores the concept of longevity in ropes from both a rigger and bottom perspective, as well as on both an immediate level and to support a longer-term practice.

Finally, Shakti discusses an essential skill set for all relationships, both in ropes and beyond: harm repair. As she says, harm is inevitable, but when repair is approached mindfully there is a real opportunity for growth and an open door to a deeper connection.

This shibari safety series is aimed at riggers and bottoms who have moved through or are familiar with the content in Safety 101, 201 and 301. These classes will add nuance, depth and essential tools to your risk-awareness in your shibari practice. Come back any time you need to brush up on these topics.
